WRO 4WS Robot - Error Catalog (1000+ Errors, Deep Detail)
=========================================================
One error entry per development morning across the whole 90-version
history repo (v1.0 -> v9.9).  Every entry includes WHAT HAPPENED,
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause / deep research), the terminal type and
exact output, and the FIX with how many days it took.

  SMALL  errors : fixed the same day (1 day)
  BIG    errors : 2-5 days, with investigation steps before the fix

Day = development-day counter only (no dates).

Total errors : 1080   (720 SMALL / 360 BIG)
Total days   : 180
Versions     : 90
Phases       : 9


----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0001 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "main.py", line 6, in <module>
      from sensors.camera import PiCamera
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first morning run of v1.x died at the first import, before a single line of robot code could execute. The whole skeleton was there, but Python refused to see it.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Python resolves packages through sys.path, and sys.path[0] is the directory of the script being run, not the current working directory. The sensors package lived under pi/, so launching from the repo root made it invisible. ModuleNotFoundError is raised at import time, which means everything after the import line is unreachable - no logs, no GPIO init, nothing.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by running the script from inside pi/, and later made permanent with sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__)) so the package resolves no matter where the script is launched from.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0002 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "main.py", line 3, in <module>
      from picamera2 import PiCamera
  ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera' from 'picamera2'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first camera test failed at import. The library was installed, so the surprise was that the symbol itself was missing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  picamera2 exports the class Picamera2 with a capital P. Python names are case-sensitive, and unlike C there is no link-time check - the failure only appears when the module is actually imported on the Pi. It never shows on the PC because the package does not exist there at all, which is exactly why this slipped past the laptop tests.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by using the exact class name Picamera2 and adding a startup import check so the mistake fails loudly and early instead of silently.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0003 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : IndentationError: unexpected indent
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 12
      print('i2c ok')
  IndentationError: unexpected indent
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning's edits crashed the script before it even started. A block that looked right in the editor was illegal to the interpreter.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The file mixed tab characters with spaces. Python 3 forbids mixing them for indentation because they are ambiguous - one tab can be 4, 8 or 12 columns depending on the editor. The parser rejects the file during compilation, so no code runs at all; the error appears the instant the script is launched.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by reformatting the block with spaces only, then setting the editor to convert tabs to 4 spaces so it can never come back.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0004 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 18, in <module>
      dev = bus.read_byte_data(addr, reg) + 'x'
  TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C scan report crashed halfway through building its output line. It had worked yesterday on the happy path, so the bug only appeared on a specific address.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  read_byte_data returns an int, and the code appended the string 'x' to it. Python is dynamically typed, so the mismatch is only detected at runtime - the line only executed for addresses that returned a value, which is why the earlier test addresses passed silently. This is a classic type-contract bug that static analyzers catch immediately.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed with str() wrapping and a review rule: every format that mixes types goes through f-strings, where the conversion is explicit.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0005 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 9, in <module>
      bus = smbus.SMBus(1)
  NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C bus scan died at the first bus access. The import line at the top of the file was there, so the name should have existed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The import statement import smbus2 was present, but the code referenced smbus. The alias was never created because the import was never written - the file used the raw package name in one place and the alias in another. NameError surfaces lazily at the first use of the name, not at import time, so the file parsed fine and only exploded mid-run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by importing smbus2 as smbus and running a quick grep for every usage to confirm no other raw references remained.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0006 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 22, in <module>
      with open('config.json') as f:
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died while reading its configuration. It worked in the repository, so the missing file only appeared once the code was deployed to the robot.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The config file was never copied to the Pi - only the code folder was synced. Worse, the path was relative, so the file location depended on the working directory at launch; systemd and cron would look in entirely different places. The error is raised by the open() syscall when the kernel returns ENOENT, and nothing in the code anticipated it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by scp'ing the config, switching to an absolute path built from the script location, and adding an explicit existence check with a clear message at boot.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0007 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 30
      if addr == 0x68:
  SyntaxError: invalid syntax
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died instantly with a parse error on a line that looked perfectly fine in the editor.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The line was missing its trailing colon - the editor's syntax highlighting had not refreshed, so the mistake was invisible. SyntaxError is raised during the compile phase before any bytecode is produced, which is why the program produced zero output; the grammar validator rejected the token stream before execution began.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the colon, and the editor was switched to save-on-format so parse errors cannot hide again.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0008 | v1.0 | SMALL | Found Day 1 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
    File "main.py", line 41, in <module>
      speed = int(input('speed: '))
  ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fast'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The manual calibration test crashed because the person at the keyboard typed a word where a number belonged.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  input() always returns a string, and int() is strict - any non-numeric character raises ValueError. The function had no validation layer, so garbage input took down the whole test harness instead of being rejected politely. This is a human-interface error, not a hardware one, but it still cost a morning because the crash aborted the calibration run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by wrapping input in try/except with a retry loop and validating the range before accepting the speed value.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0009 | v1.0 | BIG | Found Day 2 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@192.168.1.42
  ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
  $ ping 192.168.1.42
  64 bytes from 192.168.1.42: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.1 ms
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning started with an unreachable robot. Ping worked - the Pi was alive on the network - but SSH refused every connection.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  After an unclean power cut, sshd never started. The machine booted into a degraded state: networking came up, but the ssh service was disabled by the failed boot sequence. Ping (ICMP) and SSH (TCP) are completely separate paths - the Pi was reachable at layer 3 while nothing listened on port 22 at layer 4. The symptom was 'robot unreachable' but the diagnosis needed to split the network stack into layers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked ping first to separate link failure from service failure
  - Checked `systemctl status ssh` - service was dead, not starting
  - Connected via the HDMI console to start sshd manually
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by enabling ssh at boot (systemctl enable ssh) and adding a journald check to the morning script so a dead sshd is visible within seconds.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0010 | v1.0 | BIG | Found Day 2 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : Permission denied (publickey,password)
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  pi@raspberrypi: Permission denied (publickey,password).
  pi@raspberrypi's password:
  Permission denied, please try again.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH reached the Pi and asked for credentials, then rejected everything. The password that worked last week was suddenly wrong.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The default raspberry password had been changed at some point, and the new one was never recorded. SSH tries publickey first, then password; with no key installed and the wrong password, all attempts failed. The security hardening done 'to be safe' had become a brick wall because the credential was lost - a process problem, not a technical one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Tried the recorded password variants - all rejected
  - Tested if the Pi accepted keys - no key installed
  - Used the HDMI console to reset the password via sudo passwd
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by resetting the password, installing an SSH key, and writing the credentials into the project notes so a lost password can never block the robot again.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0011 | v1.0 | BIG | Found Day 2 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!
  IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!
  Host key verification failed.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH refused to connect with a security warning. The message was dramatic - 'SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY' - but the cause was mundane.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The SD card had been reflashed, which generates a new SSH host key. The PC's known_hosts file still held the old key, and SSH treats any mismatch as a possible man-in-the-middle attack. The warning is the security system working exactly as designed; the false alarm came from an undeclared reflash. Every reflash invalidates the trust record silently.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed the Pi was reimaged (the only legit cause)
  - Checked the new key fingerprint against the console
  - Removed the stale entry from known_hosts
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by running ssh-keygen -R raspberrypi to forget the old key, and adding a documented procedure that every reflash updates the key on all laptops.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0012 | v1.0 | BIG | Found Day 2 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.0/main.py
Error     : Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  [ 17.388465] Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(179,2)
  [ 17.389002] Rebooting in 5 seconds..
  ... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The Pi refused to boot, looped for ten minutes, and showed a kernel panic on the console. The robot was dead at the start of the day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  An unclean power cut corrupted the SD card's filesystem. The kernel could not mount the root partition (VFS mount failure), panicked, and rebooted into the same failure. SD cards are the most fragile component in the robot: a power drop during a write can corrupt the FAT/ext4 structures, and there is no built-in recovery. The boot loop is the kernel's only response to an unmountable root.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Watched the boot loop on the HDMI console to confirm it was a mount failure
  - Mounted the SD card on a PC to check the filesystem
  - Verified the card was physically intact with fsck
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by reflashing the SD card from the backup image, and later hardening the robot with a UPS so power cuts can never corrupt the filesystem again.

E0024 | v1.1 | BIG | Found Day 4 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.1/tools/i2c_scan.py
Error     : No space left on device while rsync'ing code
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ rsync -av pi/ pi@raspberrypi:/home/pi/robot/
  rsync: write failed: No space left on device (28)
  rsync error: some files could not be transferred (code 23)
WHAT HAPPENED
  Deploying the newest code failed halfway through. rsync reported a disk-full error and the robot ended up with a half-updated codebase - the worst state to debug.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Months of session logs and old calibration files had filled the 32GB SD card. rsync writes each file atomically but does not roll back on failure, leaving the target in a mixed state. Disk-full on a small embedded SD card is an operational hazard, not a coding error: log rotation was never configured, and nothing enforced a minimum free space.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed with df -h that the card was 100% full
  - Found 22GB of old logs in /var/log and the session folders
  - Deleted logs and verified free space before retrying
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by cleaning the logs, adding a log rotation policy, and making the deploy script abort unless at least 2GB is free.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0025 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : IndentationError: unexpected indent
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 12
      print('i2c ok')
  IndentationError: unexpected indent
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning's edits crashed the script before it even started. A block that looked right in the editor was illegal to the interpreter.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The file mixed tab characters with spaces. Python 3 forbids mixing them for indentation because they are ambiguous - one tab can be 4, 8 or 12 columns depending on the editor. The parser rejects the file during compilation, so no code runs at all; the error appears the instant the script is launched.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by reformatting the block with spaces only, then setting the editor to convert tabs to 4 spaces so it can never come back.

E0026 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 18, in <module>
      dev = bus.read_byte_data(addr, reg) + 'x'
  TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C scan report crashed halfway through building its output line. It had worked yesterday on the happy path, so the bug only appeared on a specific address.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  read_byte_data returns an int, and the code appended the string 'x' to it. Python is dynamically typed, so the mismatch is only detected at runtime - the line only executed for addresses that returned a value, which is why the earlier test addresses passed silently. This is a classic type-contract bug that static analyzers catch immediately.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed with str() wrapping and a review rule: every format that mixes types goes through f-strings, where the conversion is explicit.

E0027 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 9, in <module>
      bus = smbus.SMBus(1)
  NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C bus scan died at the first bus access. The import line at the top of the file was there, so the name should have existed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The import statement import smbus2 was present, but the code referenced smbus. The alias was never created because the import was never written - the file used the raw package name in one place and the alias in another. NameError surfaces lazily at the first use of the name, not at import time, so the file parsed fine and only exploded mid-run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by importing smbus2 as smbus and running a quick grep for every usage to confirm no other raw references remained.

E0028 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 22, in <module>
      with open('config.json') as f:
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died while reading its configuration. It worked in the repository, so the missing file only appeared once the code was deployed to the robot.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The config file was never copied to the Pi - only the code folder was synced. Worse, the path was relative, so the file location depended on the working directory at launch; systemd and cron would look in entirely different places. The error is raised by the open() syscall when the kernel returns ENOENT, and nothing in the code anticipated it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by scp'ing the config, switching to an absolute path built from the script location, and adding an explicit existence check with a clear message at boot.

E0029 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 30
      if addr == 0x68:
  SyntaxError: invalid syntax
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died instantly with a parse error on a line that looked perfectly fine in the editor.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The line was missing its trailing colon - the editor's syntax highlighting had not refreshed, so the mistake was invisible. SyntaxError is raised during the compile phase before any bytecode is produced, which is why the program produced zero output; the grammar validator rejected the token stream before execution began.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the colon, and the editor was switched to save-on-format so parse errors cannot hide again.

E0030 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 41, in <module>
      speed = int(input('speed: '))
  ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fast'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The manual calibration test crashed because the person at the keyboard typed a word where a number belonged.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  input() always returns a string, and int() is strict - any non-numeric character raises ValueError. The function had no validation layer, so garbage input took down the whole test harness instead of being rejected politely. This is a human-interface error, not a hardware one, but it still cost a morning because the crash aborted the calibration run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by wrapping input in try/except with a retry loop and validating the range before accepting the speed value.

E0031 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 6, in <module>
      from sensors.camera import PiCamera
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first morning run of v1.x died at the first import, before a single line of robot code could execute. The whole skeleton was there, but Python refused to see it.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Python resolves packages through sys.path, and sys.path[0] is the directory of the script being run, not the current working directory. The sensors package lived under pi/, so launching from the repo root made it invisible. ModuleNotFoundError is raised at import time, which means everything after the import line is unreachable - no logs, no GPIO init, nothing.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by running the script from inside pi/, and later made permanent with sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__)) so the package resolves no matter where the script is launched from.

E0032 | v1.2 | SMALL | Found Day 5 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera'
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 tools/camera_test.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "tools/camera_test.py", line 3, in <module>
      from picamera2 import PiCamera
  ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera' from 'picamera2'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first camera test failed at import. The library was installed, so the surprise was that the symbol itself was missing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  picamera2 exports the class Picamera2 with a capital P. Python names are case-sensitive, and unlike C there is no link-time check - the failure only appears when the module is actually imported on the Pi. It never shows on the PC because the package does not exist there at all, which is exactly why this slipped past the laptop tests.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by using the exact class name Picamera2 and adding a startup import check so the mistake fails loudly and early instead of silently.

E0033 | v1.2 | BIG | Found Day 6 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!
  IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!
  Host key verification failed.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH refused to connect with a security warning. The message was dramatic - 'SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY' - but the cause was mundane.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The SD card had been reflashed, which generates a new SSH host key. The PC's known_hosts file still held the old key, and SSH treats any mismatch as a possible man-in-the-middle attack. The warning is the security system working exactly as designed; the false alarm came from an undeclared reflash. Every reflash invalidates the trust record silently.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed the Pi was reimaged (the only legit cause)
  - Checked the new key fingerprint against the console
  - Removed the stale entry from known_hosts
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by running ssh-keygen -R raspberrypi to forget the old key, and adding a documented procedure that every reflash updates the key on all laptops.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0034 | v1.2 | BIG | Found Day 6 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  [ 17.388465] Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(179,2)
  [ 17.389002] Rebooting in 5 seconds..
  ... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The Pi refused to boot, looped for ten minutes, and showed a kernel panic on the console. The robot was dead at the start of the day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  An unclean power cut corrupted the SD card's filesystem. The kernel could not mount the root partition (VFS mount failure), panicked, and rebooted into the same failure. SD cards are the most fragile component in the robot: a power drop during a write can corrupt the FAT/ext4 structures, and there is no built-in recovery. The boot loop is the kernel's only response to an unmountable root.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Watched the boot loop on the HDMI console to confirm it was a mount failure
  - Mounted the SD card on a PC to check the filesystem
  - Verified the card was physically intact with fsck
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by reflashing the SD card from the backup image, and later hardening the robot with a UPS so power cuts can never corrupt the filesystem again.

E0035 | v1.2 | BIG | Found Day 6 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : No space left on device while rsync'ing code
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ rsync -av pi/ pi@raspberrypi:/home/pi/robot/
  rsync: write failed: No space left on device (28)
  rsync error: some files could not be transferred (code 23)
WHAT HAPPENED
  Deploying the newest code failed halfway through. rsync reported a disk-full error and the robot ended up with a half-updated codebase - the worst state to debug.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Months of session logs and old calibration files had filled the 32GB SD card. rsync writes each file atomically but does not roll back on failure, leaving the target in a mixed state. Disk-full on a small embedded SD card is an operational hazard, not a coding error: log rotation was never configured, and nothing enforced a minimum free space.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed with df -h that the card was 100% full
  - Found 22GB of old logs in /var/log and the session folders
  - Deleted logs and verified free space before retrying
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by cleaning the logs, adding a log rotation policy, and making the deploy script abort unless at least 2GB is free.

E0036 | v1.2 | BIG | Found Day 6 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.2/tools/camera_test.py
Error     : watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#0 stuck for 23s
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#0 stuck for 23s!
  [2345.1] Modules linked in: vl53l1x
  Call trace: [<ffff>] i2c_transfer
WHAT HAPPENED
  The Pi console froze, then the kernel watchdog fired and reported a CPU stuck for 23 seconds. The call trace pointed at the I2C driver.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L1X driver issued an I2C transfer to a broken sensor, and the I2C controller never returned. The kernel's I2C layer has no built-in timeout for this failure mode, so the driver blocked forever holding a spinlock, which froze the CPU. The watchdog exists to catch exactly this, but the root cause was a missing error path in the sensor driver combined with a hardware fault.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the call trace to confirm it was the I2C subsystem
  - Isolated the sensor bus and reproduced the hang
  - Confirmed the sensor itself was the faulty device
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by adding a bus timeout to the driver and auto-disabling the sensor after repeated failures, so one broken device can never freeze the whole system.

E0048 | v1.3 | BIG | Found Day 8 | Fixed in 5 days | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.3/esp/main/motor_test.c
Error     : esptool.FatalError: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  C:\> idf.py -p COM5 flash
  esptool.py v4.7
  Serial port COM5
  A fatal error occurred: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3: No serial data received.
WHAT HAPPENED
  Flashing the ESP32 failed instantly. The tool found the port but received no data from the chip - the connection itself was dead.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The ESP32-S3 only enters the bootloader ROM if the BOOT pin is held low during reset. If it boots normally, the ROM bootloader window closes within milliseconds and the chip answers nothing on the USB-serial interface. The wrong port was also a suspect - the board exposes two serial interfaces, and only one connects to the ROM loader. esptool's silent failure means 'no bootloader answered'.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked the device manager for which COM ports existed
  - Tried the second serial port - still silent
  - Held BOOT during reset and retried - connected instantly
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by documenting the flash procedure: hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT, then flash - and by labeling the correct COM port in flash_esp.sh.

NameError surfaces lazily at the first use of the name, not at import time, so the file parsed fine and only exploded mid-run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by importing smbus2 as smbus and running a quick grep for every usage to confirm no other raw references remained.

E0050 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 22, in <module>
      with open('config.json') as f:
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died while reading its configuration. It worked in the repository, so the missing file only appeared once the code was deployed to the robot.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0051 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 30
      if addr == 0x68:
  SyntaxError: invalid syntax
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died instantly with a parse error on a line that looked perfectly fine in the editor.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The line was missing its trailing colon - the editor's syntax highlighting had not refreshed, so the mistake was invisible. SyntaxError is raised during the compile phase before any bytecode is produced, which is why the program produced zero output; the grammar validator rejected the token stream before execution began.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the colon, and the editor was switched to save-on-format so parse errors cannot hide again.

E0052 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 41, in <module>
      speed = int(input('speed: '))
  ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fast'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The manual calibration test crashed because the person at the keyboard typed a word where a number belonged.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  input() always returns a string, and int() is strict - any non-numeric character raises ValueError. The function had no validation layer, so garbage input took down the whole test harness instead of being rejected politely. This is a human-interface error, not a hardware one, but it still cost a morning because the crash aborted the calibration run.
FIX (took 1 day)

E0053 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 6, in <module>
      from sensors.camera import PiCamera
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first morning run of v1.x died at the first import, before a single line of robot code could execute. The whole skeleton was there, but Python refused to see it.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Python resolves packages through sys.path, and sys.path[0] is the directory of the script being run, not the current working directory. The sensors package lived under pi/, so launching from the repo root made it invisible. ModuleNotFoundError is raised at import time, which means everything after the import line is unreachable - no logs, no GPIO init, nothing.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by running the script from inside pi/, and later made permanent with sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__)) so the package resolves no matter where the script is launched from.

E0054 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera'
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 3, in <module>
      from picamera2 import PiCamera
  ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera' from 'picamera2'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first camera test failed at import. The library was installed, so the surprise was that the symbol itself was missing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  picamera2 exports the class Picamera2 with a capital P. Python names are case-sensitive, and unlike C there is no link-time check - the failure only appears when the module is actually imported on the Pi. It never shows on the PC because the package does not exist there at all, which is exactly why this slipped past the laptop tests.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by using the exact class name Picamera2 and adding a startup import check so the mistake fails loudly and early instead of silently.

E0055 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : IndentationError: unexpected indent
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 12
      print('i2c ok')
  IndentationError: unexpected indent
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning's edits crashed the script before it even started. A block that looked right in the editor was illegal to the interpreter.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The file mixed tab characters with spaces. Python 3 forbids mixing them for indentation because they are ambiguous - one tab can be 4, 8 or 12 columns depending on the editor. The parser rejects the file during compilation, so no code runs at all; the error appears the instant the script is launched.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by reformatting the block with spaces only, then setting the editor to convert tabs to 4 spaces so it can never come back.

E0056 | v1.4 | SMALL | Found Day 9 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
    File "esp/main/servo_calib.c", line 18, in <module>
      dev = bus.read_byte_data(addr, reg) + 'x'
  TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C scan report crashed halfway through building its output line. It had worked yesterday on the happy path, so the bug only appeared on a specific address.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  read_byte_data returns an int, and the code appended the string 'x' to it. Python is dynamically typed, so the mismatch is only detected at runtime - the line only executed for addresses that returned a value, which is why the earlier test addresses passed silently. This is a classic type-contract bug that static analyzers catch immediately.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed with str() wrapping and a review rule: every format that mixes types goes through f-strings, where the conversion is explicit.

E0057 | v1.4 | BIG | Found Day 10 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : No space left on device while rsync'ing code
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ rsync -av pi/ pi@raspberrypi:/home/pi/robot/
  rsync: write failed: No space left on device (28)
  rsync error: some files could not be transferred (code 23)
WHAT HAPPENED
  Deploying the newest code failed halfway through. rsync reported a disk-full error and the robot ended up with a half-updated codebase - the worst state to debug.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Months of session logs and old calibration files had filled the 32GB SD card. rsync writes each file atomically but does not roll back on failure, leaving the target in a mixed state. Disk-full on a small embedded SD card is an operational hazard, not a coding error: log rotation was never configured, and nothing enforced a minimum free space.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed with df -h that the card was 100% full
  - Found 22GB of old logs in /var/log and the session folders
  - Deleted logs and verified free space before retrying
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by cleaning the logs, adding a log rotation policy, and making the deploy script abort unless at least 2GB is free.

E0058 | v1.4 | BIG | Found Day 10 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#0 stuck for 23s
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#0 stuck for 23s!
  [2345.1] Modules linked in: vl53l1x
  Call trace: [<ffff>] i2c_transfer
WHAT HAPPENED
  The Pi console froze, then the kernel watchdog fired and reported a CPU stuck for 23 seconds. The call trace pointed at the I2C driver.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L1X driver issued an I2C transfer to a broken sensor, and the I2C controller never returned. The kernel's I2C layer has no built-in timeout for this failure mode, so the driver blocked forever holding a spinlock, which froze the CPU. The watchdog exists to catch exactly this, but the root cause was a missing error path in the sensor driver combined with a hardware fault.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the call trace to confirm it was the I2C subsystem
  - Isolated the sensor bus and reproduced the hang
  - Confirmed the sensor itself was the faulty device
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by adding a bus timeout to the driver and auto-disabling the sensor after repeated failures, so one broken device can never freeze the whole system.

E0059 | v1.4 | BIG | Found Day 10 | Fixed in 4 days | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.4/esp/main/servo_calib.c
Error     : esptool.FatalError: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  C:\> idf.py -p COM5 flash
  esptool.py v4.7
  Serial port COM5
  A fatal error occurred: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3: No serial data received.
WHAT HAPPENED
  Flashing the ESP32 failed instantly. The tool found the port but received no data from the chip - the connection itself was dead.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The ESP32-S3 only enters the bootloader ROM if the BOOT pin is held low during reset. If it boots normally, the ROM bootloader window closes within milliseconds and the chip answers nothing on the USB-serial interface. The wrong port was also a suspect - the board exposes two serial interfaces, and only one connects to the ROM loader. esptool's silent failure means 'no bootloader answered'.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked the device manager for which COM ports existed
  - Tried the second serial port - still silent
  - Held BOOT during reset and retried - connected instantly
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by documenting the flash procedure: hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT, then flash - and by labeling the correct COM port in flash_esp.sh.

  $ ssh pi@192.168.1.42

  $ ping 192.168.1.42
  64 bytes from 192.168.1.42: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.1 ms
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning started with an unreachable robot. Ping worked - the Pi was alive on the network - but SSH refused every connection.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  After an unclean power cut, sshd never started. The machine booted into a degraded state: networking came up, but the ssh service was disabled by the failed boot sequence. The symptom was 'robot unreachable' but the diagnosis needed to split the network stack into layers.

  - Checked `systemctl status ssh` - service was dead, not starting
  - Connected via the HDMI console to start sshd manually
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by enabling ssh at boot (systemctl enable ssh) and adding a journald check to the morning script so a dead sshd is visible within seconds.

  The manual calibration test crashed because the person at the keyboard typed a word where a number belonged.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  input() always returns a string, and int() is strict - any non-numeric character raises ValueError. The function had no validation layer, so garbage input took down the whole test harness instead of being rejected politely. This is a human-interface error, not a hardware one, but it still cost a morning because the crash aborted the calibration run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by wrapping input in try/except with a retry loop and validating the range before accepting the speed value.

E0075 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 6, in <module>
      from sensors.camera import PiCamera
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first morning run of v1.x died at the first import, before a single line of robot code could execute. The whole skeleton was there, but Python refused to see it.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Python resolves packages through sys.path, and sys.path[0] is the directory of the script being run, not the current working directory. The sensors package lived under pi/, so launching from the repo root made it invisible. ModuleNotFoundError is raised at import time, which means everything after the import line is unreachable - no logs, no GPIO init, nothing.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by running the script from inside pi/, and later made permanent with sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__)) so the package resolves no matter where the script is launched from.

E0076 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 3, in <module>
      from picamera2 import PiCamera
  ImportError: cannot import name 'PiCamera' from 'picamera2'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first camera test failed at import. The library was installed, so the surprise was that the symbol itself was missing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  picamera2 exports the class Picamera2 with a capital P. Python names are case-sensitive, and unlike C there is no link-time check - the failure only appears when the module is actually imported on the Pi. It never shows on the PC because the package does not exist there at all, which is exactly why this slipped past the laptop tests.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by using the exact class name Picamera2 and adding a startup import check so the mistake fails loudly and early instead of silently.

E0077 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : IndentationError: unexpected indent
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 12
      print('i2c ok')
  IndentationError: unexpected indent
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning's edits crashed the script before it even started. A block that looked right in the editor was illegal to the interpreter.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The file mixed tab characters with spaces. Python 3 forbids mixing them for indentation because they are ambiguous - one tab can be 4, 8 or 12 columns depending on the editor. The parser rejects the file during compilation, so no code runs at all; the error appears the instant the script is launched.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by reformatting the block with spaces only, then setting the editor to convert tabs to 4 spaces so it can never come back.

E0078 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 18, in <module>
      dev = bus.read_byte_data(addr, reg) + 'x'
  TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C scan report crashed halfway through building its output line. It had worked yesterday on the happy path, so the bug only appeared on a specific address.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  read_byte_data returns an int, and the code appended the string 'x' to it. Python is dynamically typed, so the mismatch is only detected at runtime - the line only executed for addresses that returned a value, which is why the earlier test addresses passed silently. This is a classic type-contract bug that static analyzers catch immediately.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed with str() wrapping and a review rule: every format that mixes types goes through f-strings, where the conversion is explicit.

E0079 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 9, in <module>
      bus = smbus.SMBus(1)
  NameError: name 'smbus' is not defined
WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C bus scan died at the first bus access. The import line at the top of the file was there, so the name should have existed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The import statement import smbus2 was present, but the code referenced smbus. The alias was never created because the import was never written - the file used the raw package name in one place and the alias in another. NameError surfaces lazily at the first use of the name, not at import time, so the file parsed fine and only exploded mid-run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by importing smbus2 as smbus and running a quick grep for every usage to confirm no other raw references remained.

E0080 | v1.6 | SMALL | Found Day 13 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tools/sensor_read_all.py
    File "tools/sensor_read_all.py", line 22, in <module>
      with open('config.json') as f:
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The script died while reading its configuration. It worked in the repository, so the missing file only appeared once the code was deployed to the robot.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The config file was never copied to the Pi - only the code folder was synced. Worse, the path was relative, so the file location depended on the working directory at launch; systemd and cron would look in entirely different places. The error is raised by the open() syscall when the kernel returns ENOENT, and nothing in the code anticipated it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by scp'ing the config, switching to an absolute path built from the script location, and adding an explicit existence check with a clear message at boot.

E0081 | v1.6 | BIG | Found Day 14 | Fixed in 2 days | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : esptool.FatalError: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  C:\> idf.py -p COM5 flash
  esptool.py v4.7
  Serial port COM5
  A fatal error occurred: Failed to connect to ESP32-S3: No serial data received.
WHAT HAPPENED
  Flashing the ESP32 failed instantly. The tool found the port but received no data from the chip - the connection itself was dead.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The ESP32-S3 only enters the bootloader ROM if the BOOT pin is held low during reset. If it boots normally, the ROM bootloader window closes within milliseconds and the chip answers nothing on the USB-serial interface. The wrong port was also a suspect - the board exposes two serial interfaces, and only one connects to the ROM loader. esptool's silent failure means 'no bootloader answered'.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked the device manager for which COM ports existed
  - Tried the second serial port - still silent
  - Held BOOT during reset and retried - connected instantly
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by documenting the flash procedure: hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT, then flash - and by labeling the correct COM port in flash_esp.sh.

E0082 | v1.6 | BIG | Found Day 14 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : DHCP timeout: no WiFi address on boot
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ sudo systemctl status dhcpcd
  dhcpcd: timed out waiting for a valid DHCP server response
  eth0: no address
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot was unreachable over the network for the whole morning. On the console, the network interfaces had no addresses at all.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  At the venue the WiFi signal was too weak for a DHCP exchange, and dhcpcd timed out without falling back. Without an address the Pi was invisible to SSH, and all remote debugging was impossible. DHCP is a single point of failure in a robot that must be controllable remotely; the design assumed a DHCP server would always answer.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Attached the console to confirm the network state
  - Confirmed WiFi signal strength was marginal at the venue
  - Tested a static address - the link worked instantly
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by adding a static fallback address that dhcpcd uses when DHCP times out, and by carrying a USB-to-Ethernet adapter for a wired fallback.

E0083 | v1.6 | BIG | Found Day 14 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@192.168.1.42
  ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
  $ ping 192.168.1.42
  64 bytes from 192.168.1.42: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.1 ms
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning started with an unreachable robot. Ping worked - the Pi was alive on the network - but SSH refused every connection.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  After an unclean power cut, sshd never started. The machine booted into a degraded state: networking came up, but the ssh service was disabled by the failed boot sequence. Ping (ICMP) and SSH (TCP) are completely separate paths - the Pi was reachable at layer 3 while nothing listened on port 22 at layer 4. The symptom was 'robot unreachable' but the diagnosis needed to split the network stack into layers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked ping first to separate link failure from service failure
  - Checked `systemctl status ssh` - service was dead, not starting
  - Connected via the HDMI console to start sshd manually
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by enabling ssh at boot (systemctl enable ssh) and adding a journald check to the morning script so a dead sshd is visible within seconds.

E0084 | v1.6 | BIG | Found Day 14 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.6/tools/sensor_read_all.py
Error     : Permission denied (publickey,password)
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  pi@raspberrypi: Permission denied (publickey,password).
  pi@raspberrypi's password:
  Permission denied, please try again.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH reached the Pi and asked for credentials, then rejected everything. The password that worked last week was suddenly wrong.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The default raspberry password had been changed at some point, and the new one was never recorded. SSH tries publickey first, then password; with no key installed and the wrong password, all attempts failed. The security hardening done 'to be safe' had become a brick wall because the credential was lost - a process problem, not a technical one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Tried the recorded password variants - all rejected
  - Tested if the Pi accepted keys - no key installed
  - Used the HDMI console to reset the password via sudo passwd
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by resetting the password, installing an SSH key, and writing the credentials into the project notes so a lost password can never block the robot again.

E0096 | v1.7 | BIG | Found Day 16 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.7/hardware/led_test.py
Error     : WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!
  IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!
  Host key verification failed.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH refused to connect with a security warning. The message was dramatic - 'SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY' - but the cause was mundane.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The SD card had been reflashed, which generates a new SSH host key. The PC's known_hosts file still held the old key, and SSH treats any mismatch as a possible man-in-the-middle attack. The warning is the security system working exactly as designed; the false alarm came from an undeclared reflash. Every reflash invalidates the trust record silently.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed the Pi was reimaged (the only legit cause)
  - Checked the new key fingerprint against the console
  - Removed the stale entry from known_hosts
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by running ssh-keygen -R raspberrypi to forget the old key, and adding a documented procedure that every reflash updates the key on all laptops.

It never shows on the PC because the package does not exist there at all, which is exactly why this slipped past the laptop tests.
FIX (took 1 day)

E0100 | v1.8 | SMALL | Found Day 17 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor

WHAT HAPPENED
  The I2C scan report crashed halfway through building its output line. It had worked yesterday on the happy path, so the bug only appeared on a specific address.

E0105 | v1.8 | BIG | Found Day 18 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.8/boot.py
Error     : ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@192.168.1.42
  ssh: connect to host 192.168.1.42 port 22: Connection refused
  $ ping 192.168.1.42
  64 bytes from 192.168.1.42: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.1 ms
WHAT HAPPENED
  The morning started with an unreachable robot. Ping worked - the Pi was alive on the network - but SSH refused every connection.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  After an unclean power cut, sshd never started. The machine booted into a degraded state: networking came up, but the ssh service was disabled by the failed boot sequence. Ping (ICMP) and SSH (TCP) are completely separate paths - the Pi was reachable at layer 3 while nothing listened on port 22 at layer 4. The symptom was 'robot unreachable' but the diagnosis needed to split the network stack into layers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked ping first to separate link failure from service failure
  - Checked `systemctl status ssh` - service was dead, not starting
  - Connected via the HDMI console to start sshd manually
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by enabling ssh at boot (systemctl enable ssh) and adding a journald check to the morning script so a dead sshd is visible within seconds.

E0106 | v1.8 | BIG | Found Day 18 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal

  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi

E0107 | v1.8 | BIG | Found Day 18 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v1.8/boot.py
Error     : WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ ssh pi@raspberrypi
  WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!
  IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!
  Host key verification failed.
WHAT HAPPENED
  SSH refused to connect with a security warning. The message was dramatic - 'SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY' - but the cause was mundane.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The SD card had been reflashed, which generates a new SSH host key. The PC's known_hosts file still held the old key, and SSH treats any mismatch as a possible man-in-the-middle attack. The warning is the security system working exactly as designed; the false alarm came from an undeclared reflash. Every reflash invalidates the trust record silently.

  - Checked the new key fingerprint against the console
  - Removed the stale entry from known_hosts
FIX (took 4 days)

E0108 | v1.8 | BIG | Found Day 18 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal

  [ 17.389002] Rebooting in 5 seconds..

WHAT HAPPENED
  The Pi refused to boot, looped for ten minutes, and showed a kernel panic on the console. The robot was dead at the start of the day.

    File "main.py", line 6, in <module>
      from sensors.camera import PiCamera
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sensors'
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first morning run of v1.x died at the first import, before a single line of robot code could execute. The whole skeleton was there, but Python refused to see it.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0121 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/drive_forward.py
Error     : Wheels spin the wrong way after boot
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 drive_forward.py
  forward: left=+1.0 right=+1.0
  result: robot drives BACKWARD
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first drive test showed a robot that drove away from its operator while the log clearly said FORWARD. Hardware did what the pins said, not what the label said.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor channel macros were swapped relative to the physical wiring - channel A was driving the right motor and the code believed it was the left. PWM duty of +1 is just a number; the direction comes from the H-bridge enable pins, which were crossed. No software check can catch this; only a physical test with a known direction reveals it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by swapping the two channel macros, then adding a boot self-test that spins each wheel by name and asks a human to confirm the direction.

E0122 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/motor_driver.c
Error     : Ackermann steer angle sign is flipped in a left turn
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  left turn -> inner wheel angle +18deg
  expected inner wheel angle -18deg
WHAT HAPPENED
  The simulation produced perfect Ackermann angles, but the real robot turned the wrong way. The math was checked twice and was correct on paper.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The sign convention of the Ackermann geometry disagreed with the physical servo mounting. The robot's steering linkage pushes the wheel right when the servo angle is positive, so a mathematically positive inner-wheel angle turned the robot left. The model lived in the Pi, the mechanical convention lived in the chassis, and nothing connected the two until a physical turn test.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by negating the angle at the servo write boundary and adding a physical direction test to the turn_test script, with a comment documenting the mechanical convention.

E0123 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/uart_protocol.py
Error     : Encoder tick count stays 0
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 uart_protocol.py
  ticks: 0, 0, 0, 0
  speed: 0.00 m/s (wheel never moved)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wheel spun visibly, but the odometry reported zero ticks. The speed readout insisted the wheel was stationary while it was turning at full speed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  During rewiring, the encoder's two signal wires were swapped with the motor's power wires. The encoder needs power and a clean signal; with power and signal crossed, the interrupt pin floated and never changed state. The encoder ISR never fired, so the tick counter stayed at zero - a silent failure because no error was ever raised, just wrong data.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by matching the connector pinout against the datasheet, then adding a sanity check that raises a warning when the wheel spins with zero ticks.

  The robot surged to full speed for a moment after rolling over a bump, then recovered. The D term was the only thing that looked strange.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The derivative was computed as (error - last_error) / dt with dt=0. A bump caused two identical encoder samples with a zero time delta, dividing by zero. Python returns NaN for 0/0, and NaN propagates through every subsequent arithmetic - the PID output became NaN, which compared false against all limits, so the safety clamp never triggered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a low-pass filter on the D term and replacing the division with a guarded version that keeps the previous value when dt is below a threshold.

E0125 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/motor_driver.c
Error     : Gyro reads 250 deg/s idle
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  gyro: 248.3 deg/s  (expected ~0)
  imu status: SUSPECT
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot sat perfectly still on the bench while the gyro claimed it was spinning at 248 degrees per second - a quarter of a full rotation per second, standing still.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 was running at its default full-scale range with factory offsets. E0126 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/uart_protocol.py
Error     : Keyboard control ignores held keys
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 uart_protocol.py
  key 'w' not detected during 'a' hold
  robot turns but never speeds up
WHAT HAPPENED
  Manual driving felt broken: holding 'w' while turning did nothing, even though the key worked alone. The robot turned, but never accelerated.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The keyboard handler used a blocking read, so while one key was held, the handler waited for that key to be released before reading the next. The terminal delivers one event at a time; a blocking getch() cannot represent two simultaneous keys. This is a fundamental limitation of line-buffered terminal input, not a bug in the key table.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to raw mode with a non-blocking poll and maintaining a key-state table, which records every pressed key and merges them each control tick.

E0127 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/drive_forward.py
Error     : Duty value out of range 0-1023
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  E (312) ledc: duty out of range!
  E (312) ledc: duty=4095, max=1023
  abort() was called at PC 0x42012345
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first motor spin aborted the ESP32. The duty value was huge, and the LEDC driver refused it immediately.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The PWM timer was configured with 10-bit resolution (max 1023) but the speed calculation produced 14-bit values up to 4095. The mismatch came from two headers defining the resolution differently - pwm_config.h said 10 bits while the speed table was written for 14. The abort() is a hard assert inside the driver, by design: an out-of-range duty would produce undefined PWM behavior, so the firmware kills itself rather than corrupt the motors.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by clamping the duty in one place inside speed_control.c and asserting the resolution constant at boot, so both sides can never disagree again.

E0128 | v2.0 | SMALL | Found Day 21 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/motor_driver.c
Error     : Signed char overflow in speed command
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ idf.py monitor
  I (401) uart: MOTOR left=200 right=-30
  E (402) motor: speed 200 overflows int8
  motor stuck at 127
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor ran at half speed during calibration and ignored the requested value of 200. The command had clearly been received - it was printed in the log.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The UART parser stored speeds in an int8_t, whose maximum is 127. The value 200 overflowed to -56, which the driver then clamped to 127. The bug was a protocol/schema mismatch: the Pi generated a text protocol with no stated range, and the ESP32 guessed the width. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so in principle anything could have happened - here it produced a silently wrong motor command.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by widening the parser to int16_t, adding a range check that rejects speeds outside -100..100, and documenting the protocol range in the header.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0129 | v2.0 | BIG | Found Day 22 | Fixed in 2 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/drive_forward.py
Error     : Brownout detector was triggered
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (1200) esp_core_dump_flash: Core dump flash config is corrupted
  Brownout detector was triggered
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 rebooted exactly when both motors started. Every motor start killed the firmware in a loop.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The battery sagged below the ESP32's brownout threshold (about 2.8V) the moment both motors drew current. The brownout detector is a hardware safety circuit: when the supply dips, it holds the chip in reset. The reboot loop is the detector doing its job - the real failure was the power architecture: no bulk capacitance, thin power wires, and no low-battery cutoff.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Measured the supply voltage during motor start with a scope
  - Saw the sag to 2.6V exactly at the brownout event
  - Tested with a bench supply - no reboot, confirming the battery sag
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by adding a 1000uF capacitor across the supply, thicker power wiring, and a low-voltage cutoff that refuses to start the motors below 3.2V.

E0130 | v2.0 | BIG | Found Day 22 | Fixed in 3 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/motor_driver.c
Error     : rst:0x10 (RTCWDT_RTC_RESET), boot:0x13 (SPI_FAST_FLASH_BOOT)
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  rst:0x10 (RTCWDT_RTC_RESET), boot:0x13 (SPI_FAST_FLASH_BOOT)
  load:0x3fff0030,len:1184
  load:0x40078000,len:13260
  -> watchdog reset, boot loop
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 reset itself at random moments and rebooted. The reset reason code RTCWDT_RTC_RESET revealed the watchdog as the killer.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor task blocked on an I2C read that never completed, so it never yielded to the scheduler and never fed the task watchdog. After the configured timeout, the watchdog forced a reset - the system was not crashed, it was deadlocked, and the watchdog was the recovery mechanism. The I2C read had no timeout, which is what allowed the block to become infinite.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Decoded the reset reason from the boot banner
  - Confirmed the watchdog fired on the motor task specifically
  - Reproduced by inserting a blocked sensor read mid-run
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by adding a timeout to the I2C read and feeding the watchdog in the motor task, so a blocked bus cannot kill the loop.

E0131 | v2.0 | BIG | Found Day 22 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/uart_protocol.py
Error     : serial.serialutil.SerialException: device reports readiness to read but returned no data
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 final_drive.py
  serial.serialutil.SerialException: device reports readiness to read but returned no data
    File "pi/comm/uart.py", line 44, in read
WHAT HAPPENED
  The drive script crashed at startup on a strange serial error - the device said it had data, but the read returned nothing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The USB-UART adapter was half-seated, so the kernel's tty layer believed the device was present (it reported readability) while the adapter actually returned nothing. SerialException is raised when the read violates its own contract.   - Checked dmesg for USB disconnects during the run
  - Added a retry to see if the error was transient
FIX (took 4 days)

E0132 | v2.0 | BIG | Found Day 22 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.0/drive_forward.py
Error     : W (515) ledc: duty set to 0 due to illegal duty 4095
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  W (515) ledc: duty set to 0 due to illegal duty 4095
  motor stopped at full throttle
  code continued running
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor died at full throttle without any crash. The code kept running - the motor simply stopped obeying.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A signed int overflow turned a valid duty into 4095 - beyond the 12-bit LEDC limit - and the driver, rather than clamping, set the output to 0 as a safe default. The overflow came from a negative speed being negated at the boundary of int16. The failure was silent because a warning is not an error: the driver protected the hardware at the cost of the software's expectations.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Spotted the warning line in a flood of normal log output
  - Traced the duty value back to a negated int16 speed
  - Reproduced with the speed at the exact boundary value
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by clamping the duty in speed_control.c before the driver call and asserting that the internal speed range can never overflow int16.

E0133 | v2.1 | SMALL | Found Day 23 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.1/ackermann.py
Error     : Ackermann steer angle sign is flipped in a left turn
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 ackermann.py
  left turn -> inner wheel angle +18deg
  expected inner wheel angle -18deg
WHAT HAPPENED
  The simulation produced perfect Ackermann angles, but the real robot turned the wrong way. The math was checked twice and was correct on paper.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The sign convention of the Ackermann geometry disagreed with the physical servo mounting. The robot's steering linkage pushes the wheel right when the servo angle is positive, so a mathematically positive inner-wheel angle turned the robot left. The model lived in the Pi, the mechanical convention lived in the chassis, and nothing connected the two until a physical turn test.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by negating the angle at the servo write boundary and adding a physical direction test to the turn_test script, with a comment documenting the mechanical convention.

E0134 | v2.1 | SMALL | Found Day 23 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal

WHAT HAPPENED

  I (401) uart: MOTOR left=200 right=-30
  E (402) motor: speed 200 overflows int8
  motor stuck at 127
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor ran at half speed during calibration and ignored the requested value of 200. The command had clearly been received - it was printed in the log.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The UART parser stored speeds in an int8_t, whose maximum is 127. The value 200 overflowed to -56, which the driver then clamped to 127. The bug was a protocol/schema mismatch: the Pi generated a text protocol with no stated range, and the ESP32 guessed the width. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so in principle anything could have happened - here it produced a silently wrong motor command.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by widening the parser to int16_t, adding a range check that rejects speeds outside -100..100, and documenting the protocol range in the header.

E0151 | v2.2 | SMALL | Found Day 25 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/pwm_config.h
Error     : Wheels spin the wrong way after boot
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 pwm_config.h
  forward: left=+1.0 right=+1.0
  result: robot drives BACKWARD
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first drive test showed a robot that drove away from its operator while the log clearly said FORWARD. Hardware did what the pins said, not what the label said.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor channel macros were swapped relative to the physical wiring - channel A was driving the right motor and the code believed it was the left. PWM duty of +1 is just a number; the direction comes from the H-bridge enable pins, which were crossed. No software check can catch this; only a physical test with a known direction reveals it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by swapping the two channel macros, then adding a boot self-test that spins each wheel by name and asks a human to confirm the direction.
