E0152 | v2.2 | SMALL | Found Day 25 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/speed_control.c
Error     : Ackermann steer angle sign is flipped in a left turn
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ idf.py monitor
  left turn -> inner wheel angle +18deg
  expected inner wheel angle -18deg
WHAT HAPPENED
  The simulation produced perfect Ackermann angles, but the real robot turned the wrong way. The math was checked twice and was correct on paper.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The sign convention of the Ackermann geometry disagreed with the physical servo mounting. The robot's steering linkage pushes the wheel right when the servo angle is positive, so a mathematically positive inner-wheel angle turned the robot left. The model lived in the Pi, the mechanical convention lived in the chassis, and nothing connected the two until a physical turn test.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by negating the angle at the servo write boundary and adding a physical direction test to the turn_test script, with a comment documenting the mechanical convention.

E0153 | v2.2 | BIG | Found Day 26 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/pwm_config.h
Error     : serial.serialutil.SerialException: device reports readiness to read but returned no data
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 final_drive.py
  serial.serialutil.SerialException: device reports readiness to read but returned no data
    File "pi/comm/uart.py", line 44, in read
WHAT HAPPENED
  The drive script crashed at startup on a strange serial error - the device said it had data, but the read returned nothing.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The USB-UART adapter was half-seated, so the kernel's tty layer believed the device was present (it reported readability) while the adapter actually returned nothing. SerialException is raised when the read violates its own contract. Intermittent physical connections produce exactly this class of bizarre error: the software and the device disagree about the hardware state.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Reinserted the adapter - the error vanished, confirming the hardware
  - Checked dmesg for USB disconnects during the run
  - Added a retry to see if the error was transient
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by reseating the adapter and adding a retry-with-backoff around the read, with a clear 'check USB connection' message after three failures.

E0154 | v2.2 | BIG | Found Day 26 | Fixed in 3 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/speed_control.c
Error     : W (515) ledc: duty set to 0 due to illegal duty 4095
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  W (515) ledc: duty set to 0 due to illegal duty 4095
  motor stopped at full throttle
  code continued running
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor died at full throttle without any crash. The code kept running - the motor simply stopped obeying.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A signed int overflow turned a valid duty into 4095 - beyond the 12-bit LEDC limit - and the driver, rather than clamping, set the output to 0 as a safe default. The overflow came from a negative speed being negated at the boundary of int16. The failure was silent because a warning is not an error: the driver protected the hardware at the cost of the software's expectations.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Spotted the warning line in a flood of normal log output
  - Traced the duty value back to a negated int16 speed
  - Reproduced with the speed at the exact boundary value
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by clamping the duty in speed_control.c before the driver call and asserting that the internal speed range can never overflow int16.

E0155 | v2.2 | BIG | Found Day 26 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/speed_control.h
Error     : Odometry drift of 0.6m over a 2m run
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  run distance: 2.0m  odometry: 2.6m
  error: +0.6m (30%)
  wheelbase calibration off
WHAT HAPPENED
  The odometry claimed the robot traveled 2.6m when it actually traveled 2.0m. Every distance estimate was inflated by 30%.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

  - Computed the correction factor from the measured distance

E0156 | v2.2 | BIG | Found Day 26 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.2/pwm_config.h
Error     : abort() called: asserted 'interval > 0' in servo driver
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  abort() was called at PC 0x400d1234 on core 0
  Backtrace: servo_driver.c:118 (interval > 0)
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The firmware aborted at boot right after flashing the new PWM config. The servo task was asserting that its interval was positive - and it was zero.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The new config default set the servo interval to 0, which is meaningless as a period, and the driver asserted interval > 0. E0157 | v2.3 | SMALL | Found Day 27 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.3/encoder_driver.c
Error     : PID D-term spikes to NaN after a bump
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ idf.py monitor
  error=0.002 dterm=nan
  pid output = nan
  motor ramps to full speed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot surged to full speed for a moment after rolling over a bump, then recovered. The D term was the only thing that looked strange.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The derivative was computed as (error - last_error) / dt with dt=0. A bump caused two identical encoder samples with a zero time delta, dividing by zero. Python returns NaN for 0/0, and NaN propagates through every subsequent arithmetic - the PID output became NaN, which compared false against all limits, so the safety clamp never triggered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a low-pass filter on the D term and replacing the division with a guarded version that keeps the previous value when dt is below a threshold.

E0158 | v2.3 | SMALL | Found Day 27 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.3/odometry.py
Error     : Gyro reads 250 deg/s idle
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 odometry.py
  gyro: 248.3 deg/s  (expected ~0)
  imu status: SUSPECT
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot sat perfectly still on the bench while the gyro claimed it was spinning at 248 degrees per second - a quarter of a full rotation per second, standing still.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 was running at its default full-scale range with factory offsets. Factory gyro offsets are rarely zero, and the raw value is scaled by the full-scale constant - with the 250 dps range selected the bias of the sensor element maps to tens of degrees per second. Calibration is not a refinement, it is a prerequisite: without the bias subtraction the reading is meaningless.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by writing the calibrated offset registers during init and re-running the v3.1 calibration whenever the board or mounting changes.

E0159 | v2.3 | SMALL | Found Day 27 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.3/encoder_driver.c
Error     : Keyboard control ignores held keys
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ idf.py monitor
  key 'w' not detected during 'a' hold
  robot turns but never speeds up
WHAT HAPPENED
  Manual driving felt broken: holding 'w' while turning did nothing, even though the key worked alone. The robot turned, but never accelerated.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The keyboard handler used a blocking read, so while one key was held, the handler waited for that key to be released before reading the next. The terminal delivers one event at a time; a blocking getch() cannot represent two simultaneous keys. This is a fundamental limitation of line-buffered terminal input, not a bug in the key table.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to raw mode with a non-blocking poll and maintaining a key-state table, which records every pressed key and merges them each control tick.

E0160 | v2.3 | SMALL | Found Day 27 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.3/odometry.py
Error     : Duty value out of range 0-1023
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ idf.py monitor
  E (312) ledc: duty out of range!
  E (312) ledc: duty=4095, max=1023
  abort() was called at PC 0x42012345
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first motor spin aborted the ESP32. The duty value was huge, and the LEDC driver refused it immediately.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The PWM timer was configured with 10-bit resolution (max 1023) but the speed calculation produced 14-bit values up to 4095. The mismatch came from two headers defining the resolution differently - pwm_config.h said 10 bits while the speed table was written for 14. The abort() is a hard assert inside the driver, by design: an out-of-range duty would produce undefined PWM behavior, so the firmware kills itself rather than corrupt the motors.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by clamping the duty in one place inside speed_control.c and asserting the resolution constant at boot, so both sides can never disagree again.

E0168 | v2.3 | BIG | Found Day 28 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.3/odometry.py
Error     : Guru Meditation Error: Core 1 panic'ed (LoadProhibited)
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  Guru Meditation Error: Core 1 panic'ed (LoadProhibited)
  addr 0x00000008, cause 'load'
  Backtrace: 0x4201abce:0x3ffb1f50 motor_driver_set
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 crashed and rebooted in a loop every time a motor command arrived. The backtrace pointed at motor_driver_set, and the fault address 0x8 is a classic null-pointer dereference.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A UART command could arrive before the motor driver was initialized, so motor_driver_set() was called with a NULL handle and dereferenced the struct member at offset 8 - hence address 0x8. The ESP32's MMU traps the load, panics with Guru Meditation, and the watchdog reboots into the same race. The bug is a missing initialization ordering contract, not a random crash: the UART task and the init code had no synchronization.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the backtrace to identify motor_driver_set as the faulting function
  - Found the NULL handle was caused by an early UART command
  - Reproduced reliably by sending a command within 100ms of boot
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by null-checking the driver handle in every entry point, and by deferring the UART task start until after motor init completes.

Error     : PID D-term spikes to NaN after a bump
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ idf.py monitor
  error=0.002 dterm=nan
  pid output = nan
  motor ramps to full speed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot surged to full speed for a moment after rolling over a bump, then recovered. The D term was the only thing that looked strange.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The derivative was computed as (error - last_error) / dt with dt=0. A bump caused two identical encoder samples with a zero time delta, dividing by zero. Python returns NaN for 0/0, and NaN propagates through every subsequent arithmetic - the PID output became NaN, which compared false against all limits, so the safety clamp never triggered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a low-pass filter on the D term and replacing the division with a guarded version that keeps the previous value when dt is below a threshold.

E0177 | v2.4 | BIG | Found Day 30 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.4/gyro_reader.py
Error     : Odometry drift of 0.6m over a 2m run
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  run distance: 2.0m  odometry: 2.6m
  error: +0.6m (30%)
  wheelbase calibration off
WHAT HAPPENED
  The odometry claimed the robot traveled 2.6m when it actually traveled 2.0m. Every distance estimate was inflated by 30%.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The wheelbase constant came from the CAD model, not from the physical robot. Odometry converts wheel speeds to distance using the wheelbase and wheel diameter; a 15% error in the wheelbase produces a proportional error in the estimate. The CAD model had idealized dimensions that the 3D-printed chassis did not match - tolerance, print shrink, and assembly gaps added up to 30%.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Ran the straight-line test three times to measure the constant error
  - Measured the true wheelbase with a caliper
  - Computed the correction factor from the measured distance
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by measuring the true wheelbase and wheel diameter, updating odometry.py with the measured constants, and adding a 2m straight-line verification to the test suite.

E0178 | v2.4 | BIG | Found Day 30 | Fixed in 3 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.4/imu_driver.c
Error     : abort() called: asserted 'interval > 0' in servo driver
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  abort() was called at PC 0x400d1234 on core 0
  Backtrace: servo_driver.c:118 (interval > 0)
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The firmware aborted at boot right after flashing the new PWM config. The servo task was asserting that its interval was positive - and it was zero.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The new config default set the servo interval to 0, which is meaningless as a period, and the driver asserted interval > 0. An assert is a programming contract: the configuration violated an invariant the driver depends on. The boot order loaded the config after the servo task started, so the task observed the default value instead of the configured one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the abort message and backtrace to find the assert
  - Checked the config default for the servo interval field
  - Traced the boot order between config load and task start
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by validating the config at boot before starting the servo task and rejecting interval <= 0 with a readable error instead of an abort.

E0179 | v2.4 | BIG | Found Day 30 | Fixed in 4 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.4/pid_straight.py
Error     : Guru Meditation Error: Core 1 panic'ed (LoadProhibited)
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  Guru Meditation Error: Core 1 panic'ed (LoadProhibited)
  addr 0x00000008, cause 'load'
  Backtrace: 0x4201abce:0x3ffb1f50 motor_driver_set
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 crashed and rebooted in a loop every time a motor command arrived. The backtrace pointed at motor_driver_set, and the fault address 0x8 is a classic null-pointer dereference.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A UART command could arrive before the motor driver was initialized, so motor_driver_set() was called with a NULL handle and dereferenced the struct member at offset 8 - hence address 0x8. The ESP32's MMU traps the load, panics with Guru Meditation, and the watchdog reboots into the same race. The bug is a missing initialization ordering contract, not a random crash: the UART task and the init code had no synchronization.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the backtrace to identify motor_driver_set as the faulting function
  - Found the NULL handle was caused by an early UART command
  - Reproduced reliably by sending a command within 100ms of boot
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by null-checking the driver handle in every entry point, and by deferring the UART task start until after motor init completes.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0180 | v2.4 | BIG | Found Day 30 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.4/gyro_reader.py
Error     : E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
  E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
  motor command stream garbled
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor motion became jerky and the console filled with buffer-full errors. Commands were arriving faster than they could be consumed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The Pi sent control commands at 100Hz, but the ESP32 UART task only read the buffer once per control tick and processed each byte individually. The default RX buffer (256 bytes) overflowed between reads, and the driver discarded the overflow. This is a producer/consumer mismatch: the producer rate was known (100Hz) but the buffer depth and read granularity were never sized to it.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Counted the errors per second and correlated with command rate
  - Measured the read interval of the UART task
  - Calculated the required buffer depth from the protocol frame size
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by raising the RX buffer to 2048 bytes and reading the buffer in bulk (read_available into a local array) once per task tick.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0181 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/command_scheduler.py
Error     : Keyboard control ignores held keys
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 command_scheduler.py
  key 'w' not detected during 'a' hold
  robot turns but never speeds up
WHAT HAPPENED
  Manual driving felt broken: holding 'w' while turning did nothing, even though the key worked alone. The robot turned, but never accelerated.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The keyboard handler used a blocking read, so while one key was held, the handler waited for that key to be released before reading the next. The terminal delivers one event at a time; a blocking getch() cannot represent two simultaneous keys. This is a fundamental limitation of line-buffered terminal input, not a bug in the key table.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to raw mode with a non-blocking poll and maintaining a key-state table, which records every pressed key and merges them each control tick.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0182 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/trajectory_open.py
Error     : Duty value out of range 0-1023
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ idf.py monitor
  E (312) ledc: duty out of range!
  E (312) ledc: duty=4095, max=1023
  abort() was called at PC 0x42012345
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first motor spin aborted the ESP32. The duty value was huge, and the LEDC driver refused it immediately.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The PWM timer was configured with 10-bit resolution (max 1023) but the speed calculation produced 14-bit values up to 4095. The mismatch came from two headers defining the resolution differently - pwm_config.h said 10 bits while the speed table was written for 14. The abort() is a hard assert inside the driver, by design: an out-of-range duty would produce undefined PWM behavior, so the firmware kills itself rather than corrupt the motors.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by clamping the duty in one place inside speed_control.c and asserting the resolution constant at boot, so both sides can never disagree again.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0183 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/command_scheduler.py
Error     : Signed char overflow in speed command
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ idf.py monitor
  I (401) uart: MOTOR left=200 right=-30
  E (402) motor: speed 200 overflows int8
  motor stuck at 127
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor ran at half speed during calibration and ignored the requested value of 200. The command had clearly been received - it was printed in the log.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The UART parser stored speeds in an int8_t, whose maximum is 127. The value 200 overflowed to -56, which the driver then clamped to 127. The bug was a protocol/schema mismatch: the Pi generated a text protocol with no stated range, and the ESP32 guessed the width. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so in principle anything could have happened - here it produced a silently wrong motor command.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by widening the parser to int16_t, adding a range check that rejects speeds outside -100..100, and documenting the protocol range in the header.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0184 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/trajectory_open.py
Error     : Wheels spin the wrong way after boot
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 trajectory_open.py
  forward: left=+1.0 right=+1.0
  result: robot drives BACKWARD
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first drive test showed a robot that drove away from its operator while the log clearly said FORWARD. Hardware did what the pins said, not what the label said.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor channel macros were swapped relative to the physical wiring - channel A was driving the right motor and the code believed it was the left. PWM duty of +1 is just a number; the direction comes from the H-bridge enable pins, which were crossed. No software check can catch this; only a physical test with a known direction reveals it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by swapping the two channel macros, then adding a boot self-test that spins each wheel by name and asks a human to confirm the direction.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0185 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/command_scheduler.py
Error     : Ackermann steer angle sign is flipped in a left turn
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 command_scheduler.py
  left turn -> inner wheel angle +18deg
  expected inner wheel angle -18deg
WHAT HAPPENED
  The simulation produced perfect Ackermann angles, but the real robot turned the wrong way. The math was checked twice and was correct on paper.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The sign convention of the Ackermann geometry disagreed with the physical servo mounting. The robot's steering linkage pushes the wheel right when the servo angle is positive, so a mathematically positive inner-wheel angle turned the robot left. The model lived in the Pi, the mechanical convention lived in the chassis, and nothing connected the two until a physical turn test.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by negating the angle at the servo write boundary and adding a physical direction test to the turn_test script, with a comment documenting the mechanical convention.

E0186 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/trajectory_open.py
Error     : Encoder tick count stays 0
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 trajectory_open.py
  ticks: 0, 0, 0, 0
  speed: 0.00 m/s (wheel never moved)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wheel spun visibly, but the odometry reported zero ticks. The speed readout insisted the wheel was stationary while it was turning at full speed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  During rewiring, the encoder's two signal wires were swapped with the motor's power wires. The encoder needs power and a clean signal; with power and signal crossed, the interrupt pin floated and never changed state. The encoder ISR never fired, so the tick counter stayed at zero - a silent failure because no error was ever raised, just wrong data.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by matching the connector pinout against the datasheet, then adding a sanity check that raises a warning when the wheel spins with zero ticks.

E0188 | v2.5 | SMALL | Found Day 31 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/trajectory_open.py
Error     : Gyro reads 250 deg/s idle
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 trajectory_open.py
  gyro: 248.3 deg/s  (expected ~0)
  imu status: SUSPECT
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot sat perfectly still on the bench while the gyro claimed it was spinning at 248 degrees per second - a quarter of a full rotation per second, standing still.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 was running at its default full-scale range with factory offsets. Factory gyro offsets are rarely zero, and the raw value is scaled by the full-scale constant - with the 250 dps range selected the bias of the sensor element maps to tens of degrees per second. Calibration is not a refinement, it is a prerequisite: without the bias subtraction the reading is meaningless.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by writing the calibrated offset registers during init and re-running the v3.1 calibration whenever the board or mounting changes.

E0192 | v2.5 | BIG | Found Day 32 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.5/trajectory_open.py
Error     : Brownout detector was triggered
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (1200) esp_core_dump_flash: Core dump flash config is corrupted
  Brownout detector was triggered
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 rebooted exactly when both motors started. Every motor start killed the firmware in a loop.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The battery sagged below the ESP32's brownout threshold (about 2.8V) the moment both motors drew current. The brownout detector is a hardware safety circuit: when the supply dips, it holds the chip in reset. The reboot loop is the detector doing its job - the real failure was the power architecture: no bulk capacitance, thin power wires, and no low-battery cutoff.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Measured the supply voltage during motor start with a scope
  - Saw the sag to 2.6V exactly at the brownout event
  - Tested with a bench supply - no reboot, confirming the battery sag
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by adding a 1000uF capacitor across the supply, thicker power wiring, and a low-voltage cutoff that refuses to start the motors below 3.2V.

The bug is a missing initialization ordering contract, not a random crash: the UART task and the init code had no synchronization.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the backtrace to identify motor_driver_set as the faulting function
  - Found the NULL handle was caused by an early UART command
  - Reproduced reliably by sending a command within 100ms of boot
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by null-checking the driver handle in every entry point, and by deferring the UART task start until after motor init completes.

E0202 | v2.6 | BIG | Found Day 34 | Fixed in 3 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.6/esp_brake.c
Error     : E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
  E (904) uart: RX buffer full - data lost
  motor command stream garbled
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor motion became jerky and the console filled with buffer-full errors. Commands were arriving faster than they could be consumed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The Pi sent control commands at 100Hz, but the ESP32 UART task only read the buffer once per control tick and processed each byte individually. The default RX buffer (256 bytes) overflowed between reads, and the driver discarded the overflow. This is a producer/consumer mismatch: the producer rate was known (100Hz) but the buffer depth and read granularity were never sized to it.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Counted the errors per second and correlated with command rate
  - Measured the read interval of the UART task
  - Calculated the required buffer depth from the protocol frame size
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by raising the RX buffer to 2048 bytes and reading the buffer in bulk (read_available into a local array) once per task tick.

E0203 | v2.6 | BIG | Found Day 34 | Fixed in 4 days | ESP32 serial monitor

File      : history/v2.6/stop_reverse.py
Error     : Brownout detector was triggered
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor

WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 rebooted exactly when both motors started. Every motor start killed the firmware in a loop.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The battery sagged below the ESP32's brownout threshold (about 2.8V) the moment both motors drew current. E0204 | v2.6 | BIG | Found Day 34 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.6/dynamic_brake.py

E0205 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/scurve_profile.py
Error     : Signed char overflow in speed command
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ idf.py monitor
  I (401) uart: MOTOR left=200 right=-30
  E (402) motor: speed 200 overflows int8
  motor stuck at 127
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor ran at half speed during calibration and ignored the requested value of 200. The command had clearly been received - it was printed in the log.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The UART parser stored speeds in an int8_t, whose maximum is 127. The value 200 overflowed to -56, which the driver then clamped to 127. The bug was a protocol/schema mismatch: the Pi generated a text protocol with no stated range, and the ESP32 guessed the width. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so in principle anything could have happened - here it produced a silently wrong motor command.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by widening the parser to int16_t, adding a range check that rejects speeds outside -100..100, and documenting the protocol range in the header.

E0206 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/speed_ramp.py
Error     : Wheels spin the wrong way after boot
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 speed_ramp.py
  forward: left=+1.0 right=+1.0
  result: robot drives BACKWARD
WHAT HAPPENED
  The first drive test showed a robot that drove away from its operator while the log clearly said FORWARD. Hardware did what the pins said, not what the label said.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor channel macros were swapped relative to the physical wiring - channel A was driving the right motor and the code believed it was the left. PWM duty of +1 is just a number; the direction comes from the H-bridge enable pins, which were crossed. No software check can catch this; only a physical test with a known direction reveals it.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by swapping the two channel macros, then adding a boot self-test that spins each wheel by name and asks a human to confirm the direction.

E0207 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/scurve_profile.py
Error     : Ackermann steer angle sign is flipped in a left turn
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 scurve_profile.py
  left turn -> inner wheel angle +18deg
  expected inner wheel angle -18deg
WHAT HAPPENED
  The simulation produced perfect Ackermann angles, but the real robot turned the wrong way. The math was checked twice and was correct on paper.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The sign convention of the Ackermann geometry disagreed with the physical servo mounting. The robot's steering linkage pushes the wheel right when the servo angle is positive, so a mathematically positive inner-wheel angle turned the robot left. The model lived in the Pi, the mechanical convention lived in the chassis, and nothing connected the two until a physical turn test.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by negating the angle at the servo write boundary and adding a physical direction test to the turn_test script, with a comment documenting the mechanical convention.

E0208 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/speed_ramp.py
Error     : Encoder tick count stays 0
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 speed_ramp.py
  ticks: 0, 0, 0, 0
  speed: 0.00 m/s (wheel never moved)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wheel spun visibly, but the odometry reported zero ticks. The speed readout insisted the wheel was stationary while it was turning at full speed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  During rewiring, the encoder's two signal wires were swapped with the motor's power wires. The encoder needs power and a clean signal; with power and signal crossed, the interrupt pin floated and never changed state. The encoder ISR never fired, so the tick counter stayed at zero - a silent failure because no error was ever raised, just wrong data.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by matching the connector pinout against the datasheet, then adding a sanity check that raises a warning when the wheel spins with zero ticks.

E0209 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/scurve_profile.py
Error     : PID D-term spikes to NaN after a bump
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 scurve_profile.py
  error=0.002 dterm=nan
  pid output = nan
  motor ramps to full speed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot surged to full speed for a moment after rolling over a bump, then recovered. The D term was the only thing that looked strange.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The derivative was computed as (error - last_error) / dt with dt=0. A bump caused two identical encoder samples with a zero time delta, dividing by zero. Python returns NaN for 0/0, and NaN propagates through every subsequent arithmetic - the PID output became NaN, which compared false against all limits, so the safety clamp never triggered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a low-pass filter on the D term and replacing the division with a guarded version that keeps the previous value when dt is below a threshold.

E0210 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/speed_ramp.py
Error     : Gyro reads 250 deg/s idle
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 speed_ramp.py
  gyro: 248.3 deg/s  (expected ~0)
  imu status: SUSPECT
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot sat perfectly still on the bench while the gyro claimed it was spinning at 248 degrees per second - a quarter of a full rotation per second, standing still.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 was running at its default full-scale range with factory offsets. Factory gyro offsets are rarely zero, and the raw value is scaled by the full-scale constant - with the 250 dps range selected the bias of the sensor element maps to tens of degrees per second. Calibration is not a refinement, it is a prerequisite: without the bias subtraction the reading is meaningless.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by writing the calibrated offset registers during init and re-running the v3.1 calibration whenever the board or mounting changes.

E0211 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.7/scurve_profile.py
Error     : Keyboard control ignores held keys
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 scurve_profile.py
  key 'w' not detected during 'a' hold
  robot turns but never speeds up
WHAT HAPPENED
  Manual driving felt broken: holding 'w' while turning did nothing, even though the key worked alone. The robot turned, but never accelerated.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The keyboard handler used a blocking read, so while one key was held, the handler waited for that key to be released before reading the next. E0212 | v2.7 | SMALL | Found Day 35 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal

E0230 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)

WHAT HAPPENED
  The wheel spun visibly, but the odometry reported zero ticks. The speed readout insisted the wheel was stationary while it was turning at full speed.

E0231 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.9/final_drive.py
Error     : PID D-term spikes to NaN after a bump
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 final_drive.py
  error=0.002 dterm=nan
  pid output = nan
  motor ramps to full speed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot surged to full speed for a moment after rolling over a bump, then recovered. The D term was the only thing that looked strange.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The derivative was computed as (error - last_error) / dt with dt=0. A bump caused two identical encoder samples with a zero time delta, dividing by zero. Python returns NaN for 0/0, and NaN propagates through every subsequent arithmetic - the PID output became NaN, which compared false against all limits, so the safety clamp never triggered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a low-pass filter on the D term and replacing the division with a guarded version that keeps the previous value when dt is below a threshold.

E0232 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)

  $ python3 performance_test.py

WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot sat perfectly still on the bench while the gyro claimed it was spinning at 248 degrees per second - a quarter of a full rotation per second, standing still.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0233 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.9/final_drive.py
Error     : Keyboard control ignores held keys
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 final_drive.py
  key 'w' not detected during 'a' hold
  robot turns but never speeds up
WHAT HAPPENED
  Manual driving felt broken: holding 'w' while turning did nothing, even though the key worked alone. The robot turned, but never accelerated.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The keyboard handler used a blocking read, so while one key was held, the handler waited for that key to be released before reading the next. E0234 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.9/performance_test.py
Error     : Duty value out of range 0-1023
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ idf.py monitor
  E (312) ledc: duty out of range!
  E (312) ledc: duty=4095, max=1023
  abort() was called at PC 0x42012345
WHAT HAPPENED
  The very first motor spin aborted the ESP32. The duty value was huge, and the LEDC driver refused it immediately.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The PWM timer was configured with 10-bit resolution (max 1023) but the speed calculation produced 14-bit values up to 4095. E0235 | v2.9 | SMALL | Found Day 39 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v2.9/final_drive.py
Error     : Signed char overflow in speed command
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ idf.py monitor
  I (401) uart: MOTOR left=200 right=-30
  E (402) motor: speed 200 overflows int8
  motor stuck at 127
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motor ran at half speed during calibration and ignored the requested value of 200. The command had clearly been received - it was printed in the log.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The UART parser stored speeds in an int8_t, whose maximum is 127. The value 200 overflowed to -56, which the driver then clamped to 127. The bug was a protocol/schema mismatch: the Pi generated a text protocol with no stated range, and the ESP32 guessed the width. Signed overflow in C is undefined behavior, so in principle anything could have happened - here it produced a silently wrong motor command.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by widening the parser to int16_t, adding a range check that rejects speeds outside -100..100, and documenting the protocol range in the header.

WHAT HAPPENED
  The distance sensor returned exactly zero on every read. Not an error, not a range value - a perfect, suspicious zero every time.

E0243 | v3.0 | SMALL | Found Day 41 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.0/log_imu.py
Error     : Wall state flips every frame
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 log_imu.py
  state: LEFT WALL, RIGHT WALL, LEFT WALL, ...
  distance jitter +-4cm
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wall-following state changed sides every single frame, making the robot oscillate between two behaviors at 10Hz. The distance was stable within a few centimeters.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The state threshold sat exactly in the middle of the sensor's noise band. A 4cm jitter crossed the threshold in both directions constantly, and the state machine had no hysteresis - no memory of the previous state to suppress rapid toggling. WHAT HAPPENED
  The IMU log script reported the sensor was absent even though it was wired and powered. The address check failed on the very first register read.

WHAT HAPPENED
  The live pitch plot showed violent spikes as if the gyro was ignored. The filter ran, but the numbers made no physical sense.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0248 | v3.0 | SMALL | Found Day 41 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor

  $ python3 mpu6050_regs.py
  mag: x=+32767 y=-32767 z=+1024
  heading: jumping 0..359
WHAT HAPPENED
  The heading readout became random noise whenever the throttle rose. At standstill it was fine; the moment the motors spun, the compass went mad.

E0252 | v3.0 | BIG | Found Day 42 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.0/mpu6050_regs.py
Error     : MPU6050 FIFO overflows after 30s
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (30000) mpu6050: FIFO overflow (2048 bytes)
  gyro data: stale frames
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every 30 seconds the gyro stream glitched. The FIFO overflow error appeared exactly at the 30-second mark, every run, like clockwork.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 buffers samples in an internal 2048-byte FIFO, and the reader drained it at 50Hz while the sensor produced at 100Hz. The drain rate was half the fill rate, so the FIFO filled exactly at the overflow point - 30 seconds at these rates. The periodic glitch was the FIFO resetting, and the periodic timing was the giveaway: a hardware error would not repeat on a precise schedule.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Noticed the glitch was perfectly periodic - rate mismatch, not hardware
  - Computed fill vs drain rates from the registers
  - Confirmed the FIFO level grew linearly between overflows
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by draining the FIFO at 200Hz (twice the sensor rate) and monitoring the FIFO level register as a health metric.

E0253 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD

File      : history/v3.1/calibrate_imu.py
Error     : ToF range error 7 (VL53L1X) floods the log
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py
  WARNING: range status 7 (signal fail)
  WARNING: range status 7 (signal fail)

WHAT HAPPENED
  The console became a waterfall of identical warnings. Within seconds the useful log was buried under thousands of identical lines.

E0254 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD

  $ python3 imu_calib.json
  state: LEFT WALL, RIGHT WALL, LEFT WALL, ...

WHAT HAPPENED
  The wall-following state changed sides every single frame, making the robot oscillate between two behaviors at 10Hz. The distance was stable within a few centimeters.

E0255 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD

Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py
  frame mean = 2.1 (near black)
  camera seems dead
WHAT HAPPENED
  The camera test produced almost entirely black frames. The sensor was alive - the log showed it was capturing - but the image was dark.

E0256 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/imu_calib.json
Error     : MPU6050 WHO_AM_I mismatch 0x00
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 imu_calib.json
  WHO_AM_I = 0x00 (expected 0x68)
  IMU not found on bus
WHAT HAPPENED
  The IMU log script reported the sensor was absent even though it was wired and powered. The address check failed on the very first register read.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 answers at 0x68 or 0x69 depending on the AD0 pin. With AD0 floating, the pin read as high at power-up and the chip moved to 0x69, while the code only probed 0x68. WHO_AM_I returning 0x00 means the device never even acknowledged - the wrong address was being addressed, so the chip stayed silent.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by pulling AD0 to ground with a resistor and adding a bus scan that discovers the device address instead of assuming it.

E0257 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD

  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py

    File "calibrate_imu.py", line 27, in load_calib
WHAT HAPPENED
  The IMU driver crashed at startup reading its calibration file. The file existed and looked complete - the schema was the problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The calibration file was produced by an older calibration script that stored the fields under different names. The loader used strict key access (calib['gyro_offset']) so a renamed key raised KeyError instantly. There was no schema version in the file and no migration path, so old and new files were indistinguishable until load time.
FIX (took 1 day)

E0258 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/imu_calib.json
Error     : Complementary filter alpha out of bounds
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 imu_calib.json
  filter_config.json: alpha=1.7
  pitch follows raw accel with spikes
WHAT HAPPENED
  The live pitch plot showed violent spikes as if the gyro was ignored. The filter ran, but the numbers made no physical sense.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The complementary filter weights gyro integration by alpha and the accelerometer by (1 - alpha). With alpha=1.7 the accelerometer weight became -0.7, so the filter was actively amplifying accelerometer noise instead of suppressing it. A typo in filter_config.json wrote 1.7 instead of 0.7, and nothing validated the config against the [0,1] domain the math requires.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by clamping alpha at load time and adding a config validator that rejects values outside [0,1] with a readable error.

E0259 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/calibrate_imu.py
Error     : Magnetometer saturates near the drive motors
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py
  mag: x=+32767 y=-32767 z=+1024
  heading: jumping 0..359
WHAT HAPPENED
  The heading readout became random noise whenever the throttle rose. At standstill it was fine; the moment the motors spun, the compass went mad.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The QMC5883L's ADC saturated at its ±32767 output limits, which means the magnetic field at the sensor exceeded its measurement range. The motor current creates a strong magnetic field a few centimeters away, and at 2cm distance the field strength is comparable to the Earth's field the sensor is trying to measure. Saturated ADC values are not noise - they are clipped, which corrupts the heading completely.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by moving the sensor 5cm from the motor wiring, adding hard-iron offset calibration, and masking the heading while the throttle exceeds a threshold.

E0260 | v3.1 | SMALL | Found Day 43 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/imu_calib.json
Error     : ToF distance frozen at 0
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 imu_calib.json
  dist: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 mm
  wall state: UNKNOWN
WHAT HAPPENED
  The distance sensor returned exactly zero on every read. Not an error, not a range value - a perfect, suspicious zero every time.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L0X boot sequence requires specific register writes with strict timing between them. The init code skipped a required 5ms delay, so the sensor never left its boot state and returned the default register value of 0. The sensor was not broken - it was never initialized. This is why vendor init sequences must be copied exactly, including every delay.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by restoring the complete init sequence with all inter-register delays, and adding a power-on self-check that verifies a non-zero reading.

E0261 | v3.1 | BIG | Found Day 44 | Fixed in 2 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/calibrate_imu.py
Error     : VL53L1X range status 4 (out of bounds) constant
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  status: 4  status: 4  status: 4
  distance frozen at 100mm
WHAT HAPPENED
  The front ToF froze at 100mm - exactly the minimum range of the sensor. The status code said 'out of bounds' on every read.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The glossy track surface produced a false early echo: the light pulse bounced back strongly from the surface itself, so the sensor believed a target was at its minimum range. Range status 4 is the sensor telling the truth about what it saw. Glossy surfaces are a known optical failure for time-of-flight sensors because the peak detection picks the wrong echo.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Tested the same sensor against a matte target - read correctly
  - Compared status codes across surfaces
  - Confirmed the frozen value matched the sensor's minimum range
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by switching to long-range mode with the peak detection tuned for low-reflectivity targets, and adding a status-code check that discards status 4 reads.

E0264 | v3.1 | BIG | Found Day 44 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.1/imu_calib.json
Error     : IMU calibration accepted garbage data
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py
  collecting... done (120 samples)
  gyro bias: 1.34 deg/s (was 0.01)
  result: worse than before
WHAT HAPPENED
  The calibration tool ran 'successfully' but produced a bias 100x worse than the previous value. The tool had no way to know the robot was being bumped while it collected.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Calibration is a statistical estimate: it averages samples to find the bias. If the robot moves during collection, the samples contain real motion plus bias, and the average is corrupted.   - Compared the sample variance between the two runs
  - Found the bump event in the session log by timestamp
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by computing the sample variance before accepting the result and requiring the robot to be still, with a 'movement detected' warning when the variance is too high.

E0276 | v3.2 | BIG | Found Day 46 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.2/filter_config.json
Error     : I2C bus lockup after sensor hot-plug
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (1234) i2c: i2c_master_cmd_begin: init error
  E (1234) i2c: bus is locked
  all sensors dead until reboot
WHAT HAPPENED
  All sensors went dead at once - not one sensor failing, the whole bus. The console said the bus itself was locked.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Unplugging a sensor while the bus was active left the I2C lines in a stuck state (a device holding SDA low, or a mid-transfer state). The ESP32's I2C controller then could not start new transfers, and it reported the bus as locked. I2C has no built-in recovery; the bus can only be unlocked by the standard 9-clock-pulse reset sequence, which the driver did not implement.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed all sensors failed simultaneously, not one by one
  - Recognized the signature: bus lockup after a hot-plug event
  - Verified a reboot recovered the bus, proving the hardware was fine
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by implementing the I2C recovery sequence (9 clock pulses on SCL, then a STOP) triggered on the first init error, and locking the sensor tray so hot-plug cannot happen.

WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The calibration file was produced by an older calibration script that stored the fields under different names. The loader used strict key access (calib['gyro_offset']) so a renamed key raised KeyError instantly. There was no schema version in the file and no migration path, so old and new files were indistinguishable until load time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding a schema version field, a default fallback for missing keys, and regenerating imu_calib.json with the new format.

E0280 | v3.3 | SMALL | Found Day 47 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/mag_calib.json
Error     : Complementary filter alpha out of bounds
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 mag_calib.json
  filter_config.json: alpha=1.7
  pitch follows raw accel with spikes
WHAT HAPPENED
  The live pitch plot showed violent spikes as if the gyro was ignored. The filter ran, but the numbers made no physical sense.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The complementary filter weights gyro integration by alpha and the accelerometer by (1 - alpha). With alpha=1.7 the accelerometer weight became -0.7, so the filter was actively amplifying accelerometer noise instead of suppressing it. E0281 | v3.3 | SMALL | Found Day 47 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/heading.py
Error     : Magnetometer saturates near the drive motors
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 heading.py
  mag: x=+32767 y=-32767 z=+1024
  heading: jumping 0..359
WHAT HAPPENED
  The heading readout became random noise whenever the throttle rose. At standstill it was fine; the moment the motors spun, the compass went mad.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The QMC5883L's ADC saturated at its ±32767 output limits, which means the magnetic field at the sensor exceeded its measurement range. The motor current creates a strong magnetic field a few centimeters away, and at 2cm distance the field strength is comparable to the Earth's field the sensor is trying to measure. Saturated ADC values are not noise - they are clipped, which corrupts the heading completely.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by moving the sensor 5cm from the motor wiring, adding hard-iron offset calibration, and masking the heading while the throttle exceeds a threshold.

E0282 | v3.3 | SMALL | Found Day 47 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/mag_calib.json
Error     : ToF distance frozen at 0
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 mag_calib.json
  dist: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 mm
  wall state: UNKNOWN
WHAT HAPPENED
  The distance sensor returned exactly zero on every read. Not an error, not a range value - a perfect, suspicious zero every time.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L0X boot sequence requires specific register writes with strict timing between them. The init code skipped a required 5ms delay, so the sensor never left its boot state and returned the default register value of 0. The sensor was not broken - it was never initialized. This is why vendor init sequences must be copied exactly, including every delay.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by restoring the complete init sequence with all inter-register delays, and adding a power-on self-check that verifies a non-zero reading.

E0283 | v3.3 | SMALL | Found Day 47 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/heading.py
Error     : ToF range error 7 (VL53L1X) floods the log
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 heading.py
  WARNING: range status 7 (signal fail)
  WARNING: range status 7 (signal fail)
  ... 600 lines/second ...
WHAT HAPPENED
  The console became a waterfall of identical warnings. Within seconds the useful log was buried under thousands of identical lines.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The reflective venue tile produced a weak return echo, so the VL53L1X reported range status 7 (signal fail). The error path logged at full loop rate with no throttle - 600 lines per second is simply the loop rate. Logging is I/O, and I/O at that rate saturated the serial link and starved the control loop of CPU time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed with a rate limiter that logs the error at most once per 2 seconds and counts the suppressed occurrences, mirroring the I2C fix.

E0284 | v3.3 | SMALL | Found Day 47 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/mag_calib.json
Error     : Wall state flips every frame
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 mag_calib.json
  state: LEFT WALL, RIGHT WALL, LEFT WALL, ...
  distance jitter +-4cm
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wall-following state changed sides every single frame, making the robot oscillate between two behaviors at 10Hz. The distance was stable within a few centimeters.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The state threshold sat exactly in the middle of the sensor's noise band. A 4cm jitter crossed the threshold in both directions constantly, and the state machine had no hysteresis - no memory of the previous state to suppress rapid toggling. Threshold logic without hysteresis amplifies sensor noise into state oscillation.

E0285 | v3.3 | BIG | Found Day 48 | Fixed in 2 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/heading.py
Error     : MPU6050 FIFO overflows after 30s
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (30000) mpu6050: FIFO overflow (2048 bytes)
  gyro data: stale frames
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every 30 seconds the gyro stream glitched. The FIFO overflow error appeared exactly at the 30-second mark, every run, like clockwork.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 buffers samples in an internal 2048-byte FIFO, and the reader drained it at 50Hz while the sensor produced at 100Hz. The drain rate was half the fill rate, so the FIFO filled exactly at the overflow point - 30 seconds at these rates. The periodic glitch was the FIFO resetting, and the periodic timing was the giveaway: a hardware error would not repeat on a precise schedule.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Noticed the glitch was perfectly periodic - rate mismatch, not hardware
  - Computed fill vs drain rates from the registers
  - Confirmed the FIFO level grew linearly between overflows
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by draining the FIFO at 200Hz (twice the sensor rate) and monitoring the FIFO level register as a health metric.

E0286 | v3.3 | BIG | Found Day 48 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/mag_calib.json
Error     : IMU calibration accepted garbage data
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 calibrate_imu.py
  collecting... done (120 samples)
  gyro bias: 1.34 deg/s (was 0.01)
  result: worse than before
WHAT HAPPENED
  The calibration tool ran 'successfully' but produced a bias 100x worse than the previous value. The tool had no way to know the robot was being bumped while it collected.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Calibration is a statistical estimate: it averages samples to find the bias. If the robot moves during collection, the samples contain real motion plus bias, and the average is corrupted. The tool trusted its input completely - it never checked whether the sensor was still, because stillness was an assumption, not a measurement. Garbage in, garbage out, with a success message on top.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Re-ran the calibration with the robot untouched - bias returned to 0.01
  - Compared the sample variance between the two runs
  - Found the bump event in the session log by timestamp
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by computing the sample variance before accepting the result and requiring the robot to be still, with a 'movement detected' warning when the variance is too high.

E0287 | v3.3 | BIG | Found Day 48 | Fixed in 4 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/heading.py
Error     : I2C bus lockup after sensor hot-plug
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (1234) i2c: i2c_master_cmd_begin: init error
  E (1234) i2c: bus is locked
  all sensors dead until reboot
WHAT HAPPENED
  All sensors went dead at once - not one sensor failing, the whole bus. The console said the bus itself was locked.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Unplugging a sensor while the bus was active left the I2C lines in a stuck state (a device holding SDA low, or a mid-transfer state). The ESP32's I2C controller then could not start new transfers, and it reported the bus as locked. I2C has no built-in recovery; the bus can only be unlocked by the standard 9-clock-pulse reset sequence, which the driver did not implement.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed all sensors failed simultaneously, not one by one
  - Recognized the signature: bus lockup after a hot-plug event
  - Verified a reboot recovered the bus, proving the hardware was fine
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by implementing the I2C recovery sequence (9 clock pulses on SCL, then a STOP) triggered on the first init error, and locking the sensor tray so hot-plug cannot happen.

E0288 | v3.3 | BIG | Found Day 48 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.3/mag_calib.json
Error     : Complementary filter pitch drifts during a straight
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  pitch: 0.1 -> 1.4 deg over 10s
  gyro bias never removed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The pitch angle drifted slowly upward during a straight run. The complementary filter normally holds pitch stable - the drift was a bias problem, not a filter problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The complementary filter fuses the gyro (integrated) with the accelerometer (absolute). The gyro's small bias integrates into a growing error over time, and the filter only removes it by blending in the accelerometer - but the blend weight was too small to correct a 1.34 deg/s bias. The filter assumed a calibrated gyro; the v3.1 calibration was not applied on this boot path, so the bias leaked through.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked the calibration load at boot - it was skipped on this path
  - Logged the raw gyro value to measure the actual bias
  - Applied the bias and watched the drift disappear
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by applying the calibrated bias at every boot path and adding a drift check: pitch must stay within 0.5 degrees during a 10s static test.

E0289 | v3.4 | SMALL | Found Day 49 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.4/read_tof.py
Error     : MPU6050 WHO_AM_I mismatch 0x00
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 read_tof.py
  WHO_AM_I = 0x00 (expected 0x68)
  IMU not found on bus
WHAT HAPPENED
  The IMU log script reported the sensor was absent even though it was wired and powered. The address check failed on the very first register read.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 answers at 0x68 or 0x69 depending on the AD0 pin. With AD0 floating, the pin read as high at power-up and the chip moved to 0x69, while the code only probed 0x68. WHO_AM_I returning 0x00 means the device never even acknowledged - the wrong address was being addressed, so the chip stayed silent.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by pulling AD0 to ground with a resistor and adding a bus scan that discovers the device address instead of assuming it.

Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 tof_config.py
  frame mean = 2.1 (near black)
  camera seems dead
WHAT HAPPENED
  The camera test produced almost entirely black frames. The sensor was alive - the log showed it was capturing - but the image was dark.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The camera was still in preview mode with auto-exposure running when the first capture happened. The capture raced the exposure settling, so the frame froze before the sensor adapted to the light. E0306 | v3.5 | SMALL | Found Day 51 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/wall_state.py
Error     : Wall state flips every frame
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 wall_state.py
  state: LEFT WALL, RIGHT WALL, LEFT WALL, ...
  distance jitter +-4cm
WHAT HAPPENED
  The wall-following state changed sides every single frame, making the robot oscillate between two behaviors at 10Hz. The distance was stable within a few centimeters.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0307 | v3.5 | SMALL | Found Day 51 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)

File      : history/v3.5/tof_fusion.py

Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 tof_fusion.py
  frame mean = 2.1 (near black)
  camera seems dead
WHAT HAPPENED
  The camera test produced almost entirely black frames. The sensor was alive - the log showed it was capturing - but the image was dark.

E0308 | v3.5 | SMALL | Found Day 51 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/wall_state.py
Error     : MPU6050 WHO_AM_I mismatch 0x00
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 wall_state.py
  WHO_AM_I = 0x00 (expected 0x68)
  IMU not found on bus
WHAT HAPPENED
  The IMU log script reported the sensor was absent even though it was wired and powered. The address check failed on the very first register read.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The MPU6050 answers at 0x68 or 0x69 depending on the AD0 pin. With AD0 floating, the pin read as high at power-up and the chip moved to 0x69, while the code only probed 0x68. WHO_AM_I returning 0x00 means the device never even acknowledged - the wrong address was being addressed, so the chip stayed silent.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by pulling AD0 to ground with a resistor and adding a bus scan that discovers the device address instead of assuming it.

E0309 | v3.5 | BIG | Found Day 52 | Fixed in 2 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/tof_fusion.py
Error     : I2C bus lockup after sensor hot-plug
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (1234) i2c: i2c_master_cmd_begin: init error
  E (1234) i2c: bus is locked
  all sensors dead until reboot
WHAT HAPPENED
  All sensors went dead at once - not one sensor failing, the whole bus. The console said the bus itself was locked.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  Unplugging a sensor while the bus was active left the I2C lines in a stuck state (a device holding SDA low, or a mid-transfer state). The ESP32's I2C controller then could not start new transfers, and it reported the bus as locked. I2C has no built-in recovery; the bus can only be unlocked by the standard 9-clock-pulse reset sequence, which the driver did not implement.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed all sensors failed simultaneously, not one by one
  - Recognized the signature: bus lockup after a hot-plug event
  - Verified a reboot recovered the bus, proving the hardware was fine
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by implementing the I2C recovery sequence (9 clock pulses on SCL, then a STOP) triggered on the first init error, and locking the sensor tray so hot-plug cannot happen.

E0310 | v3.5 | BIG | Found Day 52 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/wall_state.py
Error     : Complementary filter pitch drifts during a straight
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  pitch: 0.1 -> 1.4 deg over 10s
  gyro bias never removed
WHAT HAPPENED
  The pitch angle drifted slowly upward during a straight run. The complementary filter normally holds pitch stable - the drift was a bias problem, not a filter problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The complementary filter fuses the gyro (integrated) with the accelerometer (absolute). The gyro's small bias integrates into a growing error over time, and the filter only removes it by blending in the accelerometer - but the blend weight was too small to correct a 1.34 deg/s bias. The filter assumed a calibrated gyro; the v3.1 calibration was not applied on this boot path, so the bias leaked through.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked the calibration load at boot - it was skipped on this path
  - Logged the raw gyro value to measure the actual bias
  - Applied the bias and watched the drift disappear
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by applying the calibrated bias at every boot path and adding a drift check: pitch must stay within 0.5 degrees during a 10s static test.

E0311 | v3.5 | BIG | Found Day 52 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/tof_fusion.py
Error     : Mag heading unusable with the drive motors on
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  heading: 0 -> 180 -> 90 (motors on)
  heading stable (motors off)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The compass heading became random noise whenever the motors ran. With the motors off, the heading was perfect - the correlation was immediate and obvious.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The drive motors draw up to 2A, and the current in the battery wires creates a magnetic field proportional to the current. At the magnetometer's position, the motor field overwhelmed the Earth's field (about 0.5 gauss). Hard-iron calibration only removes constant offsets, and the motor field varies with throttle - it is dynamic, so no static calibration can remove it.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Ran the motor_interference_test to map heading error vs throttle
  - Moved the sensor 5cm away and repeated - error dropped sharply
  - Confirmed the field scaled with current, not position of the robot
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by moving the sensor away from the power wiring, twisting the power leads, and masking the heading whenever throttle exceeds 30%.

E0312 | v3.5 | BIG | Found Day 52 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.5/wall_state.py
Error     : All ToF sensors report 8190mm (max range)
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  left: 8190  front: 8190  right: 8190
  wall state: OPEN everywhere
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every distance sensor reported exactly 8190mm - the maximum value of the VL53L0X. The robot believed the world was empty.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L0X API returns 8190mm as the 'no valid reading' sentinel, and the read path had never called the init function. Reads on an uninitialized sensor return the default maximum, which looks like a plausible distance. Three sensors agreeing on 8190 was the clue: real measurements never agree perfectly, but a sentinel value is identical everywhere. The code confused 'no reading' with 'far away'.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Spotted all three sensors at the exact same value - impossible for real data
  - Checked the init call path - it was missing entirely
  - Verified the vendor example shows the init requirement
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by adding the missing init call and treating 8190 as 'no reading' in the fusion layer instead of a distance.

E0313 | v3.6 | SMALL | Found Day 53 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.6/camera_config.py
Error     : Complementary filter alpha out of bounds
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 camera_config.py
  filter_config.json: alpha=1.7
  pitch follows raw accel with spikes
WHAT HAPPENED
  The live pitch plot showed violent spikes as if the gyro was ignored. The filter ran, but the numbers made no physical sense.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The complementary filter weights gyro integration by alpha and the accelerometer by (1 - alpha). With alpha=1.7 the accelerometer weight became -0.7, so the filter was actively amplifying accelerometer noise instead of suppressing it. A typo in filter_config.json wrote 1.7 instead of 0.7, and nothing validated the config against the [0,1] domain the math requires.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by clamping alpha at load time and adding a config validator that rejects values outside [0,1] with a readable error.

E0314 | v3.6 | SMALL | Found Day 53 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.6/capture_frame.py
Error     : Magnetometer saturates near the drive motors
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 capture_frame.py
  mag: x=+32767 y=-32767 z=+1024
  heading: jumping 0..359
WHAT HAPPENED
  The heading readout became random noise whenever the throttle rose. At standstill it was fine; the moment the motors spun, the compass went mad.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The QMC5883L's ADC saturated at its ±32767 output limits, which means the magnetic field at the sensor exceeded its measurement range. The motor current creates a strong magnetic field a few centimeters away, and at 2cm distance the field strength is comparable to the Earth's field the sensor is trying to measure. Saturated ADC values are not noise - they are clipped, which corrupts the heading completely.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by moving the sensor 5cm from the motor wiring, adding hard-iron offset calibration, and masking the heading while the throttle exceeds a threshold.

E0315 | v3.6 | SMALL | Found Day 53 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.6/camera_config.py
Error     : ToF distance frozen at 0
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 camera_config.py
  dist: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 mm
  wall state: UNKNOWN
WHAT HAPPENED
  The distance sensor returned exactly zero on every read. Not an error, not a range value - a perfect, suspicious zero every time.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L0X boot sequence requires specific register writes with strict timing between them. The init code skipped a required 5ms delay, so the sensor never left its boot state and returned the default register value of 0. The sensor was not broken - it was never initialized. This is why vendor init sequences must be copied exactly, including every delay.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by restoring the complete init sequence with all inter-register delays, and adding a power-on self-check that verifies a non-zero reading.

Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor

WHAT HAPPENED
  The front ToF froze at 100mm - exactly the minimum range of the sensor. The status code said 'out of bounds' on every read.

  - Confirmed the frozen value matched the sensor's minimum range

  heading: 0 -> 180 -> 90 (motors on)
  heading stable (motors off)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The compass heading became random noise whenever the motors ran. With the motors off, the heading was perfect - the correlation was immediate and obvious.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The drive motors draw up to 2A, and the current in the battery wires creates a magnetic field proportional to the current. At the magnetometer's position, the motor field overwhelmed the Earth's field (about 0.5 gauss). Hard-iron calibration only removes constant offsets, and the motor field varies with throttle - it is dynamic, so no static calibration can remove it.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Ran the motor_interference_test to map heading error vs throttle
  - Moved the sensor 5cm away and repeated - error dropped sharply
  - Confirmed the field scaled with current, not position of the robot
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by moving the sensor away from the power wiring, twisting the power leads, and masking the heading whenever throttle exceeds 30%.

E0334 | v3.7 | BIG | Found Day 56 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.7/color_detect.py
Error     : All ToF sensors report 8190mm (max range)
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  left: 8190  front: 8190  right: 8190
  wall state: OPEN everywhere
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every distance sensor reported exactly 8190mm - the maximum value of the VL53L0X. The robot believed the world was empty.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The VL53L0X API returns 8190mm as the 'no valid reading' sentinel, and the read path had never called the init function. Reads on an uninitialized sensor return the default maximum, which looks like a plausible distance. Three sensors agreeing on 8190 was the clue: real measurements never agree perfectly, but a sentinel value is identical everywhere. The code confused 'no reading' with 'far away'.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Spotted all three sensors at the exact same value - impossible for real data
  - Checked the init call path - it was missing entirely
  - Verified the vendor example shows the init requirement
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by adding the missing init call and treating 8190 as 'no reading' in the fusion layer instead of a distance.

E0335 | v3.7 | BIG | Found Day 56 | Fixed in 4 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v3.7/color_calib.json
Error     : VL53L1X range status 4 (out of bounds) constant
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  status: 4  status: 4  status: 4
  distance frozen at 100mm
WHAT HAPPENED
  The front ToF froze at 100mm - exactly the minimum range of the sensor. The status code said 'out of bounds' on every read.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The glossy track surface produced a false early echo: the light pulse bounced back strongly from the surface itself, so the sensor believed a target was at its minimum range. Range status 4 is the sensor telling the truth about what it saw. Glossy surfaces are a known optical failure for time-of-flight sensors because the peak detection picks the wrong echo.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Tested the same sensor against a matte target - read correctly
  - Compared status codes across surfaces
  - Confirmed the frozen value matched the sensor's minimum range
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by switching to long-range mode with the peak detection tuned for low-reflectivity targets, and adding a status-code check that discards status 4 reads.
