E0845 | v8.0 | SMALL | Found Day 141 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.0/steer_same.py
Error     : Steering mode switch race condition
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 steer_same.py
  mode: OPPOSITE (expected CRAB)
  one-frame wrong steering at the switch
WHAT HAPPENED
  For exactly one frame at every mode switch, the robot steered with the wrong geometry. The switch itself worked - the frame in between did not.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The mode flag was written by the mission thread and read by the control thread without synchronization. The control thread could read the flag mid-update, observing a mixed state. A one-frame glitch is exactly what a data race looks like: mostly correct, occasionally wrong, impossible to reproduce on demand.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by making the mode switch atomic - the mode lives in a single int that the scheduler publishes, and the control thread reads it through a lock-free once-store.

E0846 | v8.0 | SMALL | Found Day 141 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.0/steering_common.py
Error     : Heartbeat times out on a busy CPU
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 steering_common.py
  heartbeat lost: 1500ms
  motors cut mid-run
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motors cut out for a moment in the middle of a run, then resumed. The failsafe fired, then recovered on its own - a glitch with consequences.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The heartbeat thread could not get CPU time during perception spikes, so the failsafe correctly concluded the main loop was dead and cut the motors. The failsafe is designed to be conservative: any doubt means stop. The bug was that a healthy but busy system looked dead to the heartbeat - the failure detector could not distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the heartbeat thread priority and extending the timeout to 2s, with a separate watchdog that only fires when the main loop is truly stuck.

E0849 | v8.0 | BIG | Found Day 142 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.0/steer_same.py
Error     : OOM killer kills the perception process
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_same.py
  Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (vision)
  perception dead, robot runs blind
WHAT HAPPENED
  The perception process was killed by the kernel's OOM killer mid-run. The robot kept driving - blind, because nobody noticed the process was gone.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The vision frame queue had no size limit, so under load it buffered frames without bound and consumed the Pi's RAM. When memory ran out, the kernel's OOM killer chose the largest process - the vision process. The queue was a convenience that became a memory leak the moment consumers lagged producers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked dmesg for the OOM kill - the vision process was the target
  - Measured the RSS growth - it grew linearly with queue length
  - Capped the queue and re-ran under load
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by capping the frame queue at 4 frames with drop-oldest, and adding a memory watch that logs the RSS of each process to the health monitor.

  SD card 99% full
WHAT HAPPENED
  One bad day of testing filled the SD card with 4.2GB of warning lines. The robot kept working - until the card was full and everything stopped.

  - Traced the spam to a rate-limiter regression
  - Added rotation and a disk watermark alert

E0851 | v8.0 | BIG | Found Day 142 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.0/steer_same.py
Error     : Scheduler deadlocks when a task raises
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_same.py
  scheduler: task 'vision' raised, never resumed
  all other tasks stop
WHAT HAPPENED
  One exception in the vision task froze the entire robot - every other task stopped scheduling. The failure was in the exception path, not the task.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler loop had no exception boundary around its task invocations. When vision raised, the exception propagated out of the loop, and the asyncio gather never continued, so no task ever ran again. A system of cooperating tasks is only as robust as its weakest task unless the scheduler contains each one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Reproduced with a forced exception in a test task
  - Confirmed the gather exited and nothing resumed
  - Wrapped each task call in try/except and re-ran
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by wrapping every task invocation in try/except with logging, so a failing task is isolated and the scheduler keeps running.

Error     : Track map is off by one section
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 steer_opposite.py
  section: 5 (expected 4)
  strategy picks the wrong corner
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every lap the track map believed the robot was one section further along than reality. The strategy consistently prepared the wrong corner.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The section counter incremented on both entering and exiting the section boundary line, because the boundary check ran on the transition in both directions. A line crossing is a single event, but the code detected it twice - once entering, once leaving. The off-by-one was perfectly consistent, which made it look like a constant and masked it as a real offset.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by incrementing the section only on entry, and adding a test that drives the full lap and asserts the counter ends exactly at the section count.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0860 | v8.1 | SMALL | Found Day 143 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.1/steering_common.py
Error     : Task base double-schedules a callback
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 steering_common.py
  callback ran twice per tick
  motor command overwritten
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every control tick produced two motor commands, the second overwriting the first. The motion was erratic because half the commands were stale by one tick.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  register_task was called twice for the same task ID in main - once by the module's own registration and once by the application wiring. The scheduler had no duplicate detection, so it added the callback twice. The scheduler trusted its caller; the caller did not check whether the task was already registered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by guarding register_task with a task-ID set that rejects duplicates, and logging a warning when a duplicate registration is attempted.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0861 | v8.1 | BIG | Found Day 144 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.1/steer_opposite.py
Error     : Log severity floods the disk on a bad day
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_opposite.py
  /var/log: 4.2GB of WARNING lines
  SD card 99% full
WHAT HAPPENED
  One bad day of testing filled the SD card with 4.2GB of warning lines. The robot kept working - until the card was full and everything stopped.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A rate-limit regression let the error logger write at full rate, and the log had no rotation on the embedded system. Logging is storage I/O; unbounded logging is an unbounded disk consumption. The rate limiter that had fixed the console spam did not cover the file writer.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Found the 4.2GB log and its growth rate
  - Traced the spam to a rate-limiter regression
  - Added rotation and a disk watermark alert
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by fixing the rate limiter for the file writer and adding log rotation with a 50MB cap, plus a warning when the disk crosses 90%.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0862 | v8.1 | BIG | Found Day 144 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.1/steering_common.py
Error     : Scheduler deadlocks when a task raises
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steering_common.py
  scheduler: task 'vision' raised, never resumed
  all other tasks stop
WHAT HAPPENED
  One exception in the vision task froze the entire robot - every other task stopped scheduling. The failure was in the exception path, not the task.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler loop had no exception boundary around its task invocations. When vision raised, the exception propagated out of the loop, and the asyncio gather never continued, so no task ever ran again. A system of cooperating tasks is only as robust as its weakest task unless the scheduler contains each one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Reproduced with a forced exception in a test task
  - Confirmed the gather exited and nothing resumed
  - Wrapped each task call in try/except and re-ran
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by wrapping every task invocation in try/except with logging, so a failing task is isolated and the scheduler keeps running.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0863 | v8.1 | BIG | Found Day 144 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.1/steer_opposite.py
Error     : Heartbeat failure cuts the motors at the start line
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_opposite.py
  heartbeat: FAIL (start signal)
  motors disabled for 3s
WHAT HAPPENED
  At the start signal the motors were disabled for three seconds - the failsafe fired exactly when the robot needed to move. The start burst starved the heartbeat.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  At start, the vision and fusion tasks all wake at once and consume CPU for hundreds of milliseconds. The low-priority heartbeat thread could not run within its timeout window, so the failsafe - which is supposed to catch a dead loop - caught a merely busy one. The safety system could not tell the difference, and its design made it fire on exactly this pattern.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Logged CPU usage at the start burst - the heartbeat starved
  - Confirmed the failsafe fired while the loop was healthy
  - Prioritized the heartbeat and widened the timeout
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by boosting the heartbeat to a high-priority thread with a 2s timeout, so a busy-but-healthy system never trips the failsafe.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0864 | v8.1 | BIG | Found Day 144 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.1/steering_common.py
Error     : Surprise rule change requires a reboot
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steering_common.py
  rule changed in config: not applied
  robot keeps the old strategy
WHAT HAPPENED
  The rules were changed before a round, but the robot kept playing the old strategy. The config file was correct - the robot never read it again.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  surprise_config loaded the rules once at boot and cached them in memory. Every later read returned the cached copy, so an on-the-spot rule change could only take effect after a reboot - an impossible requirement between rounds. Configuration that is read once is not configuration, it is a build-time constant.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Changed a rule and observed no effect - cached config
  - Checked the load path - it ran only at boot
  - Added a reload at each round start
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by re-reading the rules file at every round start, with a file-hash check that logs whether the active rules changed since boot.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0865 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/imu_mode_switch.py
Error     : YAML parse error in default_config.yaml
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 imu_mode_switch.py
  yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here
  config failed to load
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot refused to boot because the configuration file could not be parsed. The file looked correct to a human - the colon in a string was the problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML treats an unquoted colon followed by a space as a key/value separator. A string containing 'mode: fast' inside a value breaks the parser because it sees a nested mapping where it did not expect one. YAML is whitespace- and punctuation-sensitive in ways that are invisible to a quick read, which is why config errors show up at load time, never at edit time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by quoting the value, and adding a config validation step at boot that parses the YAML and reports the exact line of any syntax error.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0866 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/steer_crab.py
Error     : Surprise rule key is unknown
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_crab.py
  KeyError: 'pillar_logic' in surprise_config
  rules ignored, defaults used
WHAT HAPPENED
  The surprise rules loaded without error, but the pillar logic rule never took effect - the robot ran the default behavior all day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The loader read keys by an explicit allowlist, and 'pillar_logic' was not in it, so the rule was silently dropped. A missing key in a config lookup is a silent failure when the code uses .get() with a default and a crash when it uses [] - this code used a path that neither crashed nor worked. The rules file and the loader schema had drifted apart.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the key to the loader schema and logging a warning whenever a configured rule key is ignored, so silent drops become visible.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0867 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/imu_mode_switch.py
Error     : Steering mode switch race condition
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 imu_mode_switch.py
  mode: OPPOSITE (expected CRAB)
  one-frame wrong steering at the switch
WHAT HAPPENED
  For exactly one frame at every mode switch, the robot steered with the wrong geometry. The switch itself worked - the frame in between did not.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The mode flag was written by the mission thread and read by the control thread without synchronization. The control thread could read the flag mid-update, observing a mixed state. A one-frame glitch is exactly what a data race looks like: mostly correct, occasionally wrong, impossible to reproduce on demand.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by making the mode switch atomic - the mode lives in a single int that the scheduler publishes, and the control thread reads it through a lock-free once-store.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0868 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/steer_crab.py
Error     : Heartbeat times out on a busy CPU
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_crab.py
  heartbeat lost: 1500ms
  motors cut mid-run
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motors cut out for a moment in the middle of a run, then resumed. The failsafe fired, then recovered on its own - a glitch with consequences.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The heartbeat thread could not get CPU time during perception spikes, so the failsafe correctly concluded the main loop was dead and cut the motors. The failsafe is designed to be conservative: any doubt means stop. The bug was that a healthy but busy system looked dead to the heartbeat - the failure detector could not distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the heartbeat thread priority and extending the timeout to 2s, with a separate watchdog that only fires when the main loop is truly stuck.

E0869 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/imu_mode_switch.py
Error     : Health monitor false alarm on sensor 3
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 imu_mode_switch.py
  sensor 3: FAIL (3 misses)
  actually fine, just slow
WHAT HAPPENED
  The health monitor declared the ToF dead at every boot. The sensor was alive - it was just slow to warm up, and the monitor did not wait.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The failure threshold was three consecutive misses, and the ToF's warm-up period legitimately produces more than three misses before its first valid reading. The threshold was calibrated against runtime behavior, not boot behavior. A monitor with a fixed threshold cannot distinguish a boot transient from a persistent failure.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the threshold to 20 misses and adding a warm-up grace period of 5 seconds at boot, matching the measured sensor ready time.

E0872 | v8.2 | SMALL | Found Day 145 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/steer_crab.py
Error     : Log severity mapping is wrong
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_crab.py
  ERROR logged as INFO
  failures hidden in the console
WHAT HAPPENED
  Critical failures appeared in the log with the INFO level, so nobody noticed them in the morning's flood of messages. The logging was lying about importance.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The severity enum in log_severity.py and the level table in the logger used different orderings, so the numeric codes mapped to the wrong levels. The logger wrote what it was told - the mapping was corrupted upstream. Two files defining the same concept independently is a maintenance trap: they will drift until someone notices.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by defining the severity enum in the logger module itself and importing it everywhere, so only one source of truth exists.

E0876 | v8.2 | BIG | Found Day 146 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.2/steer_crab.py
Error     : Track map mismatch after the first lap
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 steer_crab.py
  map section 6/8 but lap counter says 1
  strategy uses the wrong corner data
WHAT HAPPENED
  After one lap the track map believed the robot was in section 6 while the lap counter said lap 1. The strategy prepared for the wrong corner every lap after the first.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The track map and the lap counter each maintained their own position state and updated it at different points in the pipeline. Their states were never compared, so they drifted apart silently. Two sources of truth for the same quantity will always diverge; the only question is when they are noticed.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Logged both states after lap 1 - they disagreed
  - Traced the update points - different pipeline stages
  - Merged them into a single shared lap state
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by sharing one lap-state object between the map and the counter, with a consistency assertion that fails loudly if they ever disagree.

Error     : Track map mismatch after the first lap
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 default_config.yaml
  map section 6/8 but lap counter says 1
  strategy uses the wrong corner data
WHAT HAPPENED
  After one lap the track map believed the robot was in section 6 while the lap counter said lap 1. The strategy prepared for the wrong corner every lap after the first.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The track map and the lap counter each maintained their own position state and updated it at different points in the pipeline. Their states were never compared, so they drifted apart silently. Two sources of truth for the same quantity will always diverge; the only question is when they are noticed.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Logged both states after lap 1 - they disagreed
  - Traced the update points - different pipeline stages
  - Merged them into a single shared lap state
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by sharing one lap-state object between the map and the counter, with a consistency assertion that fails loudly if they ever disagree.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0888 | v8.3 | BIG | Found Day 148 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.3/surprise_config.py
Error     : Health monitor kills the camera on a cold start
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 surprise_config.py
  camera: FAIL -> restart -> FAIL (3x)
  camera was fine after 60s
WHAT HAPPENED
  The health monitor restarted the camera three times at boot, then gave up - while the camera was simply slow to start in the cold. The monitor caused the failure it was watching for.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The camera produces no frames for the first several seconds on a cold boot. The health monitor interpreted the silence as a failure and issued a restart, and each restart reset the same cold-start condition. The monitor's retry loop amplified the boot transient into a permanent failure - the fix was the opposite of the restart it kept performing.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Noticed the camera recovered when left alone
  - Timed the cold-start delay - it exceeded the health timeout
  - Added a grace period before the first camera check
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by waiting 10 seconds before the first camera health check, and by backing off restarts exponentially instead of restarting instantly.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0889 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_config.py
Error     : Steering mode switch race condition
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_config.py
  mode: OPPOSITE (expected CRAB)
  one-frame wrong steering at the switch
WHAT HAPPENED
  For exactly one frame at every mode switch, the robot steered with the wrong geometry. The switch itself worked - the frame in between did not.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The mode flag was written by the mission thread and read by the control thread without synchronization. The control thread could read the flag mid-update, observing a mixed state. A one-frame glitch is exactly what a data race looks like: mostly correct, occasionally wrong, impossible to reproduce on demand.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by making the mode switch atomic - the mode lives in a single int that the scheduler publishes, and the control thread reads it through a lock-free once-store.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0890 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_tracker.py
Error     : Heartbeat times out on a busy CPU
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_tracker.py
  heartbeat lost: 1500ms
  motors cut mid-run
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motors cut out for a moment in the middle of a run, then resumed. The failsafe fired, then recovered on its own - a glitch with consequences.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The heartbeat thread could not get CPU time during perception spikes, so the failsafe correctly concluded the main loop was dead and cut the motors. The failsafe is designed to be conservative: any doubt means stop. The bug was that a healthy but busy system looked dead to the heartbeat - the failure detector could not distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the heartbeat thread priority and extending the timeout to 2s, with a separate watchdog that only fires when the main loop is truly stuck.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0891 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_config.py
Error     : Health monitor false alarm on sensor 3
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_config.py
  sensor 3: FAIL (3 misses)
  actually fine, just slow
WHAT HAPPENED
  The health monitor declared the ToF dead at every boot. The sensor was alive - it was just slow to warm up, and the monitor did not wait.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The failure threshold was three consecutive misses, and the ToF's warm-up period legitimately produces more than three misses before its first valid reading. The threshold was calibrated against runtime behavior, not boot behavior. A monitor with a fixed threshold cannot distinguish a boot transient from a persistent failure.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the threshold to 20 misses and adding a warm-up grace period of 5 seconds at boot, matching the measured sensor ready time.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0892 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_tracker.py
Error     : Track map is off by one section
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_tracker.py
  section: 5 (expected 4)
  strategy picks the wrong corner
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every lap the track map believed the robot was one section further along than reality. The strategy consistently prepared the wrong corner.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The section counter incremented on both entering and exiting the section boundary line, because the boundary check ran on the transition in both directions. A line crossing is a single event, but the code detected it twice - once entering, once leaving. The off-by-one was perfectly consistent, which made it look like a constant and masked it as a real offset.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by incrementing the section only on entry, and adding a test that drives the full lap and asserts the counter ends exactly at the section count.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0893 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_config.py
Error     : Task base double-schedules a callback
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_config.py
  callback ran twice per tick
  motor command overwritten
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every control tick produced two motor commands, the second overwriting the first. The motion was erratic because half the commands were stale by one tick.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  register_task was called twice for the same task ID in main - once by the module's own registration and once by the application wiring. The scheduler had no duplicate detection, so it added the callback twice. The scheduler trusted its caller; the caller did not check whether the task was already registered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by guarding register_task with a task-ID set that rejects duplicates, and logging a warning when a duplicate registration is attempted.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0894 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_tracker.py
Error     : Log severity mapping is wrong
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_tracker.py
  ERROR logged as INFO
  failures hidden in the console
WHAT HAPPENED
  Critical failures appeared in the log with the INFO level, so nobody noticed them in the morning's flood of messages. The logging was lying about importance.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The severity enum in log_severity.py and the level table in the logger used different orderings, so the numeric codes mapped to the wrong levels. The logger wrote what it was told - the mapping was corrupted upstream. Two files defining the same concept independently is a maintenance trap: they will drift until someone notices.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by defining the severity enum in the logger module itself and importing it everywhere, so only one source of truth exists.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0895 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_config.py
Error     : YAML parse error in default_config.yaml
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_config.py
  yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here
  config failed to load
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot refused to boot because the configuration file could not be parsed. The file looked correct to a human - the colon in a string was the problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML treats an unquoted colon followed by a space as a key/value separator. A string containing 'mode: fast' inside a value breaks the parser because it sees a nested mapping where it did not expect one. YAML is whitespace- and punctuation-sensitive in ways that are invisible to a quick read, which is why config errors show up at load time, never at edit time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by quoting the value, and adding a config validation step at boot that parses the YAML and reports the exact line of any syntax error.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0896 | v8.4 | SMALL | Found Day 149 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_tracker.py
Error     : Surprise rule key is unknown
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pillar_tracker.py
  KeyError: 'pillar_logic' in surprise_config
  rules ignored, defaults used
WHAT HAPPENED
  The surprise rules loaded without error, but the pillar logic rule never took effect - the robot ran the default behavior all day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The loader read keys by an explicit allowlist, and 'pillar_logic' was not in it, so the rule was silently dropped. A missing key in a config lookup is a silent failure when the code uses .get() with a default and a crash when it uses [] - this code used a path that neither crashed nor worked. The rules file and the loader schema had drifted apart.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the key to the loader schema and logging a warning whenever a configured rule key is ignored, so silent drops become visible.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0897 | v8.4 | BIG | Found Day 150 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_config.py
Error     : Surprise rule change requires a reboot
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 pillar_config.py
  rule changed in config: not applied
  robot keeps the old strategy
WHAT HAPPENED
  The rules were changed before a round, but the robot kept playing the old strategy. The config file was correct - the robot never read it again.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  surprise_config loaded the rules once at boot and cached them in memory. Every later read returned the cached copy, so an on-the-spot rule change could only take effect after a reboot - an impossible requirement between rounds. Configuration that is read once is not configuration, it is a build-time constant.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Changed a rule and observed no effect - cached config
  - Checked the load path - it ran only at boot
  - Added a reload at each round start
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by re-reading the rules file at every round start, with a file-hash check that logs whether the active rules changed since boot.

E0900 | v8.4 | BIG | Found Day 150 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.4/pillar_tracker.py
Error     : ESP32 flash with the wrong partition table
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 pillar_tracker.py
  esptool: data does not match the partition table
  ESP32 boot loops
WHAT HAPPENED
  After flashing, the ESP32 boot-looped. The flash succeeded - the app was written to a partition the partition table did not define.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The application partition had grown past the size declared in the partition table, or the table itself was for a different flash layout. The chip boots into the app region from the table; if the table does not describe the flashed layout, the bootloader cannot find the app and resets. The build and the flash layout were not validated against each other.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the boot logs - the partition entry was missing
  - Compared the partition table with the app size
  - Reflashed with the standard 4MB table
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by pinning the partition table in the project config, and adding a CI check that fails if the compiled app exceeds its partition.

E0912 | v8.5 | BIG | Found Day 152 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.5/parking_geometry.py
Error     : OOM killer kills the perception process
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 parking_geometry.py
  Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (vision)
  perception dead, robot runs blind
WHAT HAPPENED
  The perception process was killed by the kernel's OOM killer mid-run. The robot kept driving - blind, because nobody noticed the process was gone.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The vision frame queue had no size limit, so under load it buffered frames without bound and consumed the Pi's RAM. When memory ran out, the kernel's OOM killer chose the largest process - the vision process. The queue was a convenience that became a memory leak the moment consumers lagged producers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked dmesg for the OOM kill - the vision process was the target
  - Measured the RSS growth - it grew linearly with queue length
  - Capped the queue and re-ran under load
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by capping the frame queue at 4 frames with drop-oldest, and adding a memory watch that logs the RSS of each process to the health monitor.

WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  register_task was called twice for the same task ID in main - once by the module's own registration and once by the application wiring. The scheduler had no duplicate detection, so it added the callback twice. The scheduler trusted its caller; the caller did not check whether the task was already registered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by guarding register_task with a task-ID set that rejects duplicates, and logging a warning when a duplicate registration is attempted.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0916 | v8.6 | SMALL | Found Day 153 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_sections.py
Error     : Log severity mapping is wrong
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 track_sections.py
  ERROR logged as INFO
  failures hidden in the console
WHAT HAPPENED
  Critical failures appeared in the log with the INFO level, so nobody noticed them in the morning's flood of messages. The logging was lying about importance.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The severity enum in log_severity.py and the level table in the logger used different orderings, so the numeric codes mapped to the wrong levels. The logger wrote what it was told - the mapping was corrupted upstream. Two files defining the same concept independently is a maintenance trap: they will drift until someone notices.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by defining the severity enum in the logger module itself and importing it everywhere, so only one source of truth exists.

E0917 | v8.6 | SMALL | Found Day 153 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_map.py
Error     : YAML parse error in default_config.yaml
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 track_map.py
  yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here
  config failed to load
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot refused to boot because the configuration file could not be parsed. The file looked correct to a human - the colon in a string was the problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML treats an unquoted colon followed by a space as a key/value separator. A string containing 'mode: fast' inside a value breaks the parser because it sees a nested mapping where it did not expect one. YAML is whitespace- and punctuation-sensitive in ways that are invisible to a quick read, which is why config errors show up at load time, never at edit time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by quoting the value, and adding a config validation step at boot that parses the YAML and reports the exact line of any syntax error.

E0918 | v8.6 | SMALL | Found Day 153 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_sections.py
Error     : Surprise rule key is unknown
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 track_sections.py
  KeyError: 'pillar_logic' in surprise_config
  rules ignored, defaults used
WHAT HAPPENED
  The surprise rules loaded without error, but the pillar logic rule never took effect - the robot ran the default behavior all day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The loader read keys by an explicit allowlist, and 'pillar_logic' was not in it, so the rule was silently dropped. A missing key in a config lookup is a silent failure when the code uses .get() with a default and a crash when it uses [] - this code used a path that neither crashed nor worked. The rules file and the loader schema had drifted apart.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by adding the key to the loader schema and logging a warning whenever a configured rule key is ignored, so silent drops become visible.

E0919 | v8.6 | SMALL | Found Day 153 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_map.py
Error     : Steering mode switch race condition
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 track_map.py
  mode: OPPOSITE (expected CRAB)
  one-frame wrong steering at the switch
WHAT HAPPENED
  For exactly one frame at every mode switch, the robot steered with the wrong geometry. The switch itself worked - the frame in between did not.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The mode flag was written by the mission thread and read by the control thread without synchronization. The control thread could read the flag mid-update, observing a mixed state. A one-frame glitch is exactly what a data race looks like: mostly correct, occasionally wrong, impossible to reproduce on demand.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by making the mode switch atomic - the mode lives in a single int that the scheduler publishes, and the control thread reads it through a lock-free once-store.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0920 | v8.6 | SMALL | Found Day 153 | Fixed in 1 day | systemd journal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_sections.py
Error     : Heartbeat times out on a busy CPU
Terminal  : systemd journal
  $ python3 track_sections.py
  heartbeat lost: 1500ms
  motors cut mid-run
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motors cut out for a moment in the middle of a run, then resumed. The failsafe fired, then recovered on its own - a glitch with consequences.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The heartbeat thread could not get CPU time during perception spikes, so the failsafe correctly concluded the main loop was dead and cut the motors. The failsafe is designed to be conservative: any doubt means stop. The bug was that a healthy but busy system looked dead to the heartbeat - the failure detector could not distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the heartbeat thread priority and extending the timeout to 2s, with a separate watchdog that only fires when the main loop is truly stuck.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0921 | v8.6 | BIG | Found Day 154 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_map.py
Error     : Health monitor kills the camera on a cold start
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 track_map.py
  camera: FAIL -> restart -> FAIL (3x)
  camera was fine after 60s
WHAT HAPPENED
  The health monitor restarted the camera three times at boot, then gave up - while the camera was simply slow to start in the cold. The monitor caused the failure it was watching for.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The camera produces no frames for the first several seconds on a cold boot. The health monitor interpreted the silence as a failure and issued a restart, and each restart reset the same cold-start condition. The monitor's retry loop amplified the boot transient into a permanent failure - the fix was the opposite of the restart it kept performing.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Noticed the camera recovered when left alone
  - Timed the cold-start delay - it exceeded the health timeout
  - Added a grace period before the first camera check
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by waiting 10 seconds before the first camera health check, and by backing off restarts exponentially instead of restarting instantly.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0922 | v8.6 | BIG | Found Day 154 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_sections.py
Error     : ESP32 flash with the wrong partition table
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 track_sections.py
  esptool: data does not match the partition table
  ESP32 boot loops
WHAT HAPPENED
  After flashing, the ESP32 boot-looped. The flash succeeded - the app was written to a partition the partition table did not define.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The application partition had grown past the size declared in the partition table, or the table itself was for a different flash layout. The chip boots into the app region from the table; if the table does not describe the flashed layout, the bootloader cannot find the app and resets. The build and the flash layout were not validated against each other.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the boot logs - the partition entry was missing
  - Compared the partition table with the app size
  - Reflashed with the standard 4MB table
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by pinning the partition table in the project config, and adding a CI check that fails if the compiled app exceeds its partition.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0923 | v8.6 | BIG | Found Day 154 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_map.py
Error     : OOM killer kills the perception process
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 track_map.py
  Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (vision)
  perception dead, robot runs blind
WHAT HAPPENED
  The perception process was killed by the kernel's OOM killer mid-run. The robot kept driving - blind, because nobody noticed the process was gone.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The vision frame queue had no size limit, so under load it buffered frames without bound and consumed the Pi's RAM. When memory ran out, the kernel's OOM killer chose the largest process - the vision process. The queue was a convenience that became a memory leak the moment consumers lagged producers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked dmesg for the OOM kill - the vision process was the target
  - Measured the RSS growth - it grew linearly with queue length
  - Capped the queue and re-ran under load
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by capping the frame queue at 4 frames with drop-oldest, and adding a memory watch that logs the RSS of each process to the health monitor.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
E0924 | v8.6 | BIG | Found Day 154 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.6/track_sections.py
Error     : Log severity floods the disk on a bad day
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 track_sections.py
  /var/log: 4.2GB of WARNING lines
  SD card 99% full
WHAT HAPPENED
  One bad day of testing filled the SD card with 4.2GB of warning lines. The robot kept working - until the card was full and everything stopped.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  A rate-limit regression let the error logger write at full rate, and the log had no rotation on the embedded system. Logging is storage I/O; unbounded logging is an unbounded disk consumption. The rate limiter that had fixed the console spam did not cover the file writer.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Found the 4.2GB log and its growth rate
  - Traced the spam to a rate-limiter regression
  - Added rotation and a disk watermark alert
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by fixing the rate limiter for the file writer and adding log rotation with a 50MB cap, plus a warning when the disk crosses 90%.

E0925 | v8.7 | SMALL | Found Day 155 | Fixed in 1 day | VS Code terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.7/scheduler.py
Error     : Track map is off by one section
Terminal  : VS Code terminal
  $ python3 scheduler.py
  section: 5 (expected 4)
  strategy picks the wrong corner
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every lap the track map believed the robot was one section further along than reality. The strategy consistently prepared the wrong corner.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The section counter incremented on both entering and exiting the section boundary line, because the boundary check ran on the transition in both directions. A line crossing is a single event, but the code detected it twice - once entering, once leaving. The off-by-one was perfectly consistent, which made it look like a constant and masked it as a real offset.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by incrementing the section only on entry, and adding a test that drives the full lap and asserts the counter ends exactly at the section count.

E0936 | v8.7 | BIG | Found Day 156 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.7/task_base.py
Error     : Scheduler deadlocks when a task raises
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 task_base.py
  scheduler: task 'vision' raised, never resumed
  all other tasks stop
WHAT HAPPENED
  One exception in the vision task froze the entire robot - every other task stopped scheduling. The failure was in the exception path, not the task.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler loop had no exception boundary around its task invocations. When vision raised, the exception propagated out of the loop, and the asyncio gather never continued, so no task ever ran again. A system of cooperating tasks is only as robust as its weakest task unless the scheduler contains each one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Reproduced with a forced exception in a test task
  - Confirmed the gather exited and nothing resumed
  - Wrapped each task call in try/except and re-ran
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by wrapping every task invocation in try/except with logging, so a failing task is isolated and the scheduler keeps running.

Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 heartbeat_protocol.py
  section: 5 (expected 4)
  strategy picks the wrong corner
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every lap the track map believed the robot was one section further along than reality. The strategy consistently prepared the wrong corner.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The section counter incremented on both entering and exiting the section boundary line, because the boundary check ran on the transition in both directions. A line crossing is a single event, but the code detected it twice - once entering, once leaving. The off-by-one was perfectly consistent, which made it look like a constant and masked it as a real offset.
FIX (took 1 day)

E0945 | v8.8 | BIG | Found Day 158 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.8/health_monitor.py
Error     : OOM killer kills the perception process
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 health_monitor.py
  Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (vision)
  perception dead, robot runs blind
WHAT HAPPENED
  The perception process was killed by the kernel's OOM killer mid-run. The robot kept driving - blind, because nobody noticed the process was gone.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The vision frame queue had no size limit, so under load it buffered frames without bound and consumed the Pi's RAM. When memory ran out, the kernel's OOM killer chose the largest process - the vision process. The queue was a convenience that became a memory leak the moment consumers lagged producers.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Checked dmesg for the OOM kill - the vision process was the target
  - Measured the RSS growth - it grew linearly with queue length
  - Capped the queue and re-ran under load
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by capping the frame queue at 4 frames with drop-oldest, and adding a memory watch that logs the RSS of each process to the health monitor.

E0947 | v8.8 | BIG | Found Day 158 | Fixed in 4 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.8/health_monitor.py
Error     : Scheduler deadlocks when a task raises
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 health_monitor.py
  scheduler: task 'vision' raised, never resumed
  all other tasks stop
WHAT HAPPENED
  One exception in the vision task froze the entire robot - every other task stopped scheduling. The failure was in the exception path, not the task.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler loop had no exception boundary around its task invocations. When vision raised, the exception propagated out of the loop, and the asyncio gather never continued, so no task ever ran again. A system of cooperating tasks is only as robust as its weakest task unless the scheduler contains each one.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Reproduced with a forced exception in a test task
  - Confirmed the gather exited and nothing resumed
  - Wrapped each task call in try/except and re-ran
FIX (took 4 days)
  Fixed by wrapping every task invocation in try/except with logging, so a failing task is isolated and the scheduler keeps running.

E0948 | v8.8 | BIG | Found Day 158 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.8/heartbeat_protocol.py
Error     : Heartbeat failure cuts the motors at the start line
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 heartbeat_protocol.py
  heartbeat: FAIL (start signal)
  motors disabled for 3s
WHAT HAPPENED
  At the start signal the motors were disabled for three seconds - the failsafe fired exactly when the robot needed to move. The start burst starved the heartbeat.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  At start, the vision and fusion tasks all wake at once and consume CPU for hundreds of milliseconds. The low-priority heartbeat thread could not run within its timeout window, so the failsafe - which is supposed to catch a dead loop - caught a merely busy one. The safety system could not tell the difference, and its design made it fire on exactly this pattern.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Logged CPU usage at the start burst - the heartbeat starved
  - Confirmed the failsafe fired while the loop was healthy
  - Prioritized the heartbeat and widened the timeout
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by boosting the heartbeat to a high-priority thread with a 2s timeout, so a busy-but-healthy system never trips the failsafe.

E0949 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/error_logger.py
Error     : Log severity mapping is wrong
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 error_logger.py
  ERROR logged as INFO
  failures hidden in the console
WHAT HAPPENED
  Critical failures appeared in the log with the INFO level, so nobody noticed them in the morning's flood of messages. The logging was lying about importance.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The severity enum in log_severity.py and the level table in the logger used different orderings, so the numeric codes mapped to the wrong levels. The logger wrote what it was told - the mapping was corrupted upstream. Two files defining the same concept independently is a maintenance trap: they will drift until someone notices.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by defining the severity enum in the logger module itself and importing it everywhere, so only one source of truth exists.

E0950 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/log_severity.py
Error     : YAML parse error in default_config.yaml
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 log_severity.py
  yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here
  config failed to load
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot refused to boot because the configuration file could not be parsed. The file looked correct to a human - the colon in a string was the problem.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML treats an unquoted colon followed by a space as a key/value separator. A string containing 'mode: fast' inside a value breaks the parser because it sees a nested mapping where it did not expect one. YAML is whitespace- and punctuation-sensitive in ways that are invisible to a quick read, which is why config errors show up at load time, never at edit time.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by quoting the value, and adding a config validation step at boot that parses the YAML and reports the exact line of any syntax error.

E0951 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/error_logger.py
Error     : Surprise rule key is unknown
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 error_logger.py
  KeyError: 'pillar_logic' in surprise_config
  rules ignored, defaults used
WHAT HAPPENED
  The surprise rules loaded without error, but the pillar logic rule never took effect - the robot ran the default behavior all day.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The loader read keys by an explicit allowlist, and 'pillar_logic' was not in it, so the rule was silently dropped. A missing key in a config lookup is a silent failure when the code uses .get() with a default and a crash when it uses [] - this code used a path that neither crashed nor worked. The rules file and the loader schema had drifted apart.
FIX (took 1 day)

E0952 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/log_severity.py
Error     : Steering mode switch race condition
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 log_severity.py
  mode: OPPOSITE (expected CRAB)
  one-frame wrong steering at the switch
WHAT HAPPENED
  For exactly one frame at every mode switch, the robot steered with the wrong geometry. The switch itself worked - the frame in between did not.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The mode flag was written by the mission thread and read by the control thread without synchronization. The control thread could read the flag mid-update, observing a mixed state. A one-frame glitch is exactly what a data race looks like: mostly correct, occasionally wrong, impossible to reproduce on demand.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by making the mode switch atomic - the mode lives in a single int that the scheduler publishes, and the control thread reads it through a lock-free once-store.

E0953 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/error_logger.py
Error     : Heartbeat times out on a busy CPU
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 error_logger.py
  heartbeat lost: 1500ms
  motors cut mid-run
WHAT HAPPENED
  The motors cut out for a moment in the middle of a run, then resumed. The failsafe fired, then recovered on its own - a glitch with consequences.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The heartbeat thread could not get CPU time during perception spikes, so the failsafe correctly concluded the main loop was dead and cut the motors. The failsafe is designed to be conservative: any doubt means stop. The bug was that a healthy but busy system looked dead to the heartbeat - the failure detector could not distinguish 'slow' from 'dead'.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the heartbeat thread priority and extending the timeout to 2s, with a separate watchdog that only fires when the main loop is truly stuck.

E0954 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/log_severity.py
Error     : Health monitor false alarm on sensor 3
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 log_severity.py
  sensor 3: FAIL (3 misses)
  actually fine, just slow
WHAT HAPPENED
  The health monitor declared the ToF dead at every boot. The sensor was alive - it was just slow to warm up, and the monitor did not wait.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The failure threshold was three consecutive misses, and the ToF's warm-up period legitimately produces more than three misses before its first valid reading. The threshold was calibrated against runtime behavior, not boot behavior. A monitor with a fixed threshold cannot distinguish a boot transient from a persistent failure.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by raising the threshold to 20 misses and adding a warm-up grace period of 5 seconds at boot, matching the measured sensor ready time.

E0956 | v8.9 | SMALL | Found Day 159 | Fixed in 1 day | Pi console (HDMI)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/log_severity.py
Error     : Task base double-schedules a callback
Terminal  : Pi console (HDMI)
  $ python3 log_severity.py
  callback ran twice per tick
  motor command overwritten
WHAT HAPPENED
  Every control tick produced two motor commands, the second overwriting the first. The motion was erratic because half the commands were stale by one tick.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  register_task was called twice for the same task ID in main - once by the module's own registration and once by the application wiring. The scheduler had no duplicate detection, so it added the callback twice. The scheduler trusted its caller; the caller did not check whether the task was already registered.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by guarding register_task with a task-ID set that rejects duplicates, and logging a warning when a duplicate registration is attempted.

E0960 | v8.9 | BIG | Found Day 160 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v8.9/log_severity.py
Error     : Surprise rule change requires a reboot
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 log_severity.py
  rule changed in config: not applied
  robot keeps the old strategy
WHAT HAPPENED
  The rules were changed before a round, but the robot kept playing the old strategy. The config file was correct - the robot never read it again.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  surprise_config loaded the rules once at boot and cached them in memory. Every later read returned the cached copy, so an on-the-spot rule change could only take effect after a reboot - an impossible requirement between rounds. Configuration that is read once is not configuration, it is a build-time constant.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Changed a rule and observed no effect - cached config
  - Checked the load path - it ran only at boot
  - Added a reload at each round start
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by re-reading the rules file at every round start, with a file-hash check that logs whether the active rules changed since boot.

E0961 | v9.0 | SMALL | Found Day 161 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/esp_main.c
Error     : Lint failure in CI on unused import
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ idf.py monitor
  flake8: F401 'sys' imported but unused
  CI job failed in 8s
WHAT HAPPENED
  The CI pipeline went red 8 seconds after the push. The failure was a single unused import - trivial, but it blocked the whole pipeline.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The final cleanup left 'import sys' after removing the code that used it. flake8's F401 rule flags any unused import, and the CI gate treated warnings as failures. A lint failure is the cheapest possible error to catch - it costs seconds - which is exactly why the gate exists: to catch before the hardware run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by removing the import, and by running flake8 locally before pushing so the CI gate never sees the mistake.

E0962 | v9.0 | SMALL | Found Day 161 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/pi_main.py
Error     : setup.cfg ignores the pi package
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pi_main.py
  pytest: no tests ran
  test_full_pipeline skipped
WHAT HAPPENED
  The CI reported success while running zero tests. A green pipeline is only as good as the tests it actually runs.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  setup.cfg listed packages manually and pi.* was missing, so pytest's package discovery found no test modules and exited with code 0 - an empty success. An empty test run looks exactly like a passing run to a CI system that only checks the exit code. The configuration and the codebase had diverged when the pi/ tree was reorganized.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to packages = find: so discovery is automatic, and adding a CI assertion that the test count is greater than zero.

E0963 | v9.0 | SMALL | Found Day 161 | Fixed in 1 day | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/esp_main.c
Error     : LED pin conflict with the camera
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ idf.py monitor
  led: 0 0 0  (camera init fails)
  camera and LED share a pin
WHAT HAPPENED
  The status LED was dead and the camera failed to initialize - two unrelated-looking failures that shared one cause.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The LED was wired to the camera's enable pin, so driving the LED pulled the camera's enable line low. Each subsystem's config named the pin differently ('led_gpio' vs 'camera_enable'), so the conflict was invisible in the config review. The two features shared a physical resource that no single file owned.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by moving the LED to a spare GPIO and adding a pin-conflict check at boot that rejects two peripherals claiming the same GPIO.

Error     : Surprise rule YAML has a duplicate key
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  $ python3 pi_main.py
  yaml.constructor.DuplicateKeyError
  config load aborts
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot failed to boot on race morning because the rules file had the same key twice. A merge conflict had duplicated a line and no one noticed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML strictly forbids duplicate keys, and the parser raises DuplicateKeyError - the loader correctly refused to guess which value wins. The duplicate came from a bad merge that produced two pillar_logic entries. YAML's strictness here is a feature: silently picking one of two conflicting values would be worse.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by removing the duplicate, and adding a pre-merge check that parses every YAML file and rejects duplicates in CI.

  $ idf.py monitor

  timing-dependent assertion
WHAT HAPPENED
  The full-pipeline test failed on the first run of the morning and passed every run after. A cold Pi is a different computer than a warm one.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)

E0969 | v9.0 | BIG | Found Day 162 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/esp_main.c
Error     : Full pipeline crashes 2 seconds after the start
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "main.py", line 88, in <module>
      scheduler.start()
    File "pi/system/scheduler.py", line 31
      await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
  TypeError: 'Task' object is not callable
WHAT HAPPENED
  The final integrated system crashed two seconds after launch - after all subsystems had started successfully. The crash was in the scheduler, the last piece to start.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler defined a class named Task, shadowing asyncio.Task inside the module. asyncio.gather expects coroutine objects or Tasks; it received the module's own Task class instance, which is not awaitable, raising TypeError. The name collision was invisible until the exact code path that combined both symbols executed - which only happens at the very end of startup.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Read the traceback - the scheduler line and the class name matched
  - Checked asyncio.gather's requirements against the argument
  - Renamed the internal class and verified the whole startup
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by renaming the internal class to ScheduledTask, and adding a smoke test that runs the full startup sequence before every race.

E0970 | v9.0 | BIG | Found Day 162 | Fixed in 3 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/pi_main.py
Error     : Camera frozen at the race morning start
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
  frame: identical for 40s
  camera driver: no error, no frame
WHAT HAPPENED
  On race morning the camera output a single frozen frame for 40 seconds. No error, no exception - just a frame that never changed, while the robot drove blind.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The camera read call had no timeout, so when the sensor stalled (a known cold-start quirk of the camera module), the driver blocked forever inside read(). Blocking reads fail silently by design: the code waits, nothing happens, no signal is raised. The pipeline kept consuming the last frame, so the system looked alive while being blind.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed the frame was a single frame repeated, not a new capture
  - Checked the driver - the read had no timeout
  - Added a timeout that raises after 2s of no frame
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by adding a 2-second read timeout that triggers a camera restart, and logging 'camera frozen' when a restart occurs.

E0971 | v9.0 | BIG | Found Day 162 | Fixed in 4 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.0/esp_main.c
Error     : ESP32 watchdog resets during the final run
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (89430) task_wdt: Task watchdog got triggered
  task: motor_ctrl did not reset the watchdog
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 rebooted in the middle of the final run - 89 seconds in, the motor task had not fed its watchdog. The loop restarted the robot at full speed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor task blocked on a UART write with no timeout: the Pi stopped reading (its own CPU was saturated), the ESP32's TX buffer filled, and the write waited forever. A blocked write means no watchdog feed, and the hardware watchdog correctly reset the system. Two independent saturation problems met in one blocking call.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Decoded the watchdog message - the motor task was the victim
  - Logged the UART write - it blocked when the Pi stopped reading
  - Made the write non-blocking with a timeout
FIX (took 4 days)

E0973 | v9.1 | SMALL | Found Day 163 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/pi_main.py
Error     : setup.cfg ignores the pi package
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 pi_main.py
  pytest: no tests ran
  test_full_pipeline skipped
WHAT HAPPENED
  The CI reported success while running zero tests. A green pipeline is only as good as the tests it actually runs.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  setup.cfg listed packages manually and pi.* was missing, so pytest's package discovery found no test modules and exited with code 0 - an empty success. An empty test run looks exactly like a passing run to a CI system that only checks the exit code. The configuration and the codebase had diverged when the pi/ tree was reorganized.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to packages = find: so discovery is automatic, and adding a CI assertion that the test count is greater than zero.

E0974 | v9.1 | SMALL | Found Day 163 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/main.py
Error     : LED pin conflict with the camera
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 main.py
  led: 0 0 0  (camera init fails)
  camera and LED share a pin
WHAT HAPPENED
  The status LED was dead and the camera failed to initialize - two unrelated-looking failures that shared one cause.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The LED was wired to the camera's enable pin, so driving the LED pulled the camera's enable line low. Each subsystem's config named the pin differently ('led_gpio' vs 'camera_enable'), so the conflict was invisible in the config review. The two features shared a physical resource that no single file owned.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by moving the LED to a spare GPIO and adding a pin-conflict check at boot that rejects two peripherals claiming the same GPIO.

E0975 | v9.1 | SMALL | Found Day 163 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/pi_main.py
Error     : Surprise rule YAML has a duplicate key
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 pi_main.py
  yaml.constructor.DuplicateKeyError
  config load aborts
WHAT HAPPENED
  The robot failed to boot on race morning because the rules file had the same key twice. A merge conflict had duplicated a line and no one noticed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  YAML strictly forbids duplicate keys, and the parser raises DuplicateKeyError - the loader correctly refused to guess which value wins. The duplicate came from a bad merge that produced two pillar_logic entries. YAML's strictness here is a feature: silently picking one of two conflicting values would be worse.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by removing the duplicate, and adding a pre-merge check that parses every YAML file and rejects duplicates in CI.

E0976 | v9.1 | SMALL | Found Day 163 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/main.py
Error     : Test flaky on the first run of the day
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 main.py
  FAILED test_full_pipeline - passed 5 minutes later
  timing-dependent assertion
WHAT HAPPENED
  The full-pipeline test failed on the first run of the morning and passed every run after. A cold Pi is a different computer than a warm one.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The test asserted that the pipeline reaches 100Hz within 2 seconds of start. A cold Pi takes longer to warm up its clocks and caches, so the first run of the day missed the deadline. Timing assertions embed an assumption about the machine state, and machine state varies with temperature and uptime.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by relaxing the assertion to a 20% margin and measuring the warm-up time over a week of first runs to set a realistic bound.

E0977 | v9.1 | SMALL | Found Day 163 | Fixed in 1 day | Windows CMD
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/pi_main.py
Error     : Lint failure in CI on unused import
Terminal  : Windows CMD
  $ python3 pi_main.py
  flake8: F401 'sys' imported but unused
  CI job failed in 8s
WHAT HAPPENED
  The CI pipeline went red 8 seconds after the push. The failure was a single unused import - trivial, but it blocked the whole pipeline.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The final cleanup left 'import sys' after removing the code that used it. flake8's F401 rule flags any unused import, and the CI gate treated warnings as failures. A lint failure is the cheapest possible error to catch - it costs seconds - which is exactly why the gate exists: to catch before the hardware run.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by removing the import, and by running flake8 locally before pushing so the CI gate never sees the mistake.

E0981 | v9.1 | BIG | Found Day 164 | Fixed in 2 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/pi_main.py
Error     : Camera frozen at the race morning start
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ python3 main.py
  frame: identical for 40s
  camera driver: no error, no frame
WHAT HAPPENED
  On race morning the camera output a single frozen frame for 40 seconds. No error, no exception - just a frame that never changed, while the robot drove blind.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The camera read call had no timeout, so when the sensor stalled (a known cold-start quirk of the camera module), the driver blocked forever inside read(). Blocking reads fail silently by design: the code waits, nothing happens, no signal is raised. The pipeline kept consuming the last frame, so the system looked alive while being blind.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Confirmed the frame was a single frame repeated, not a new capture
  - Checked the driver - the read had no timeout
  - Added a timeout that raises after 2s of no frame
FIX (took 2 days)
  Fixed by adding a 2-second read timeout that triggers a camera restart, and logging 'camera frozen' when a restart occurs.

E0982 | v9.1 | BIG | Found Day 164 | Fixed in 3 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/main.py
Error     : ESP32 watchdog resets during the final run
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  E (89430) task_wdt: Task watchdog got triggered
  task: motor_ctrl did not reset the watchdog
  Rebooting... (loop)
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 rebooted in the middle of the final run - 89 seconds in, the motor task had not fed its watchdog. The loop restarted the robot at full speed.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The motor task blocked on a UART write with no timeout: the Pi stopped reading (its own CPU was saturated), the ESP32's TX buffer filled, and the write waited forever. A blocked write means no watchdog feed, and the hardware watchdog correctly reset the system. Two independent saturation problems met in one blocking call.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Decoded the watchdog message - the motor task was the victim
  - Logged the UART write - it blocked when the Pi stopped reading
  - Made the write non-blocking with a timeout
FIX (took 3 days)
  Fixed by setting the UART write to non-blocking with a 10ms timeout, and feeding the watchdog before every write so a stalled link cannot stall the loop.

E0984 | v9.1 | BIG | Found Day 164 | Fixed in 5 days | ESP32 serial monitor
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.1/main.py
Error     : Core dump triggered: store data at 0x3ffb0e10
Terminal  : ESP32 serial monitor
  Core 0 panic'ed (StoreProhibited)
  store data at 0x3ffb0e10, pc 0x400df220
  Backtrace: 0x400df220:0x3ffb1f30 scheduler_tick
WHAT HAPPENED
  The ESP32 crashed with a StoreProhibited panic - a write to protected memory. The backtrace pointed at the scheduler, of all places.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The scheduler task wrote to a task context that had been freed: a task was deleted, its memory returned to the heap, and the scheduler still held a pointer to it. A use-after-free is a memory bug that appears at the moment the allocator reuses the freed block - which is why it only crashed under specific timing.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Decoded the panic - StoreProhibited at the scheduler tick
  - Traced the pointer - it referenced a deleted task
  - Deferred task deletion to the idle hook
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by deferring task deletion to the idle hook so the scheduler never touches freed contexts, and adding a task-count assertion at every delete.

E0996 | v9.2 | BIG | Found Day 166 | Fixed in 5 days | Pi SSH terminal
----------------------------------------------------------------------
File      : history/v9.2/pillar_detector.py
Error     : Race day: SD card corrupt after the power cut
Terminal  : Pi SSH terminal
  $ journalctl
  ext4-fs error (device mmcblk0p2)
  Remounting filesystem read-only
  python3: can't open file 'main.py'
WHAT HAPPENED
  On race day the SD card was corrupted by the power cut during the previous night's calibration. The filesystem remounted read-only and the robot could not even start Python.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  The Pi was powered off without a clean shutdown, and the ext4 journal could not replay, leaving the filesystem in an inconsistent state. ext4 responded by remounting read-only to protect the data. A robot that is powered off by pulling the battery is a robot that will eventually lose its filesystem - the shutdown was an operational habit, and it became a race-day failure.
INVESTIGATION (before the fix)
  - Mounted the card on a PC and ran fsck
  - Recovered the code from the backup image
  - Converted the root filesystem to read-only with an overlay for logs
FIX (took 5 days)
  Fixed by switching to a read-only rootfs with a RAM-backed log overlay, so power cuts can never corrupt the boot filesystem again.

  pytest: no tests ran
  test_full_pipeline skipped
WHAT HAPPENED
  The CI reported success while running zero tests. A green pipeline is only as good as the tests it actually runs.
WHY IT HAPPENED (root cause)
  setup.cfg listed packages manually and pi.* was missing, so pytest's package discovery found no test modules and exited with code 0 - an empty success. An empty test run looks exactly like a passing run to a CI system that only checks the exit code. The configuration and the codebase had diverged when the pi/ tree was reorganized.
FIX (took 1 day)
  Fixed by switching to packages = find: so discovery is automatic, and adding a CI assertion that the test count is greater than zero.
